entry.title: THE FINAL OUT FALLS UPON THE BUFFET INSTEAD: RAYS 5, PADRES 4, IN ELEVEN INNINGS
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 54 · Monday, the One-and-Thirtieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 14 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE FINAL OUT FALLS UPON THE BUFFET INSTEAD: RAYS 5, PADRES 4, IN ELEVEN INNINGS

Two out in the ninth, two runs down, and the left fielder Taylor gloves the last fly ball at the warning track — whereupon the low wall of Tropicana Field, carved down a generation ago for the convenience of home-run thieves, performs its old trick in reverse: the ball spills from the glove onto the buffet tables beyond, a game-tying two-run homer for DeLuca by way of the defense itself, and two innings later Mateo lines the winning single as Tampa Bay completes its record-tying fourteenth sweep of the season

The ball game at Tropicana Field ended twice on Sunday before it consented to end properly. The first ending came with two out in the ninth, the Sunshine nine trailing three runs to one with Caminero aboard, when Jonny DeLuca lifted the untouchable Mason Miller's offering to the left-field corner and Samad Taylor ran it down at the warning track, glove outstretched, the final out apparently secured. But Taylor's momentum carried him into the lower portion of the wall — the very section cut down years ago so that Carl Crawford might more easily rob homers, the section that made Longoria's Game 162 blast of legend possible — and as he struck the fence the ball hopped free of the leather and dropped upon the 162 Landing buffet on the far side. A game-tying two-run homer, delivered by the defense's own hand. "Obviously," said DeLuca, "I love that wall." Taylor kept his own books differently: "I don't know if it goes down as an error in the books, but in my mind, it's an error. It hit my glove and should be caught."

The arithmetic against that ninth inning had been nearly absolute. San Diego stood nine-and-fifty wins and no defeats this season when leading after eight innings; Tampa Bay stood two wins and eight-and-forty defeats when trailing after them; and only two men had taken Miller over a fence since he first drew a San Diego paycheck a summer ago. Caminero, whose leadoff single began the resurrection, pronounced the verdict from first base the moment the ball dropped: "I said, 'Oh, the game's over right there. We're winning no matter what.'" The prophecy required two more innings' patience. The San Diego nine pushed their free runner across in the eleventh by wild pitch and France's sacrifice fly, whereupon the home half answered in kind and then some: Hicks singled, the pinch-runner Piper stole second, Simpson was walked intentionally to load the bases, and DeLuca's bouncer to short was bobbled by Bogaerts, the tying run scoring — before Jorge Mateo lined the first walk-off hit of his major-league life over Taylor's head in left. "It feels great," said Mateo. "I wish that it was like that every single day."

The ledger takes the full measure of the afternoon. The sweep of San Diego is Tampa Bay's fourteenth of the season, most in all baseball and the equal of the franchise record; the winning streak runs to four; and at two-and-eighty wins against four-and-fifty defeats the Rays keep the American's best record, their lead in the East four games and a half over New York. Caminero's seven-and-thirtieth homer, struck off the left-hander Ray in the fourth, draws him dead level with Houston's Alvarez atop the American's home-run table. "That's probably the most exciting one we've had this year," ruled the starter Rasmussen, and the manager Cash, who learned the ball was over the wall only when "everybody started yelling at me," did not dispute it. The Pads depart swept clean out of Tampa Bay, half a game now separating them from Arizona's wild-card chair, their afternoon further vexed by the seventh inning's ejections — the protocol desk below has that correspondence. The clubs part ways this evening: the Mets call at the Trop at 6:40, while San Diego opens at Cincinnati.

News Around the League

THE MILESTONE DESK: AT TWO-AND-FORTY YEARS, SCHERZER CLIMBS PAST PERRY INTO NINTH ON THE ALL-TIME STRIKEOUT LEDGER — AND RAMÍREZ CREEPS UPON TWO ROUND NUMBERS AT ONCE

Max Scherzer, aged two-and-forty years and four-and-thirty days, chose Sunday in Toronto to remind the almanac he is still writing in it. Ten strikeouts across seven innings — a single hit and a single walk against them, as the card below relates — carried his career count to three thousand five hundred five-and-thirty, past the late spitballer Gaylord Perry and into ninth place on the all-time strikeout ledger. It was, the researchers add, the hundred-and-fifteenth game of ten strikeouts or better in Scherzer's long life, a total exceeded only by Nolan Ryan's 215 and Randy Johnson's 212. "I respect who's on this list," said the old campaigner. "To be moving up the top 10 all-time means something." The Herald, which has lately made a habit of chronicling the elder statesmen — Sale's shutout Thursday, Skubal's homecoming Friday — enters Mad Max's Sunday beside them with pleasure.

The desk notes a quieter pair of approaching round numbers in Cleveland: José Ramírez's two-run homer in Sunday's rout — his first over a fence since the sixth of June, a five-week exile for a fractured hamate bone intervening — brings his career accounts to 296 homers and 997 runs batted in, four blasts and three runs driven home shy of the three-hundred-and-one-thousand pairing that would place him among the game's most select company. "When you get that guy going, we all go," testified his young pitcher Messick.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: ELLY'S QUADRICEPS SOUNDS AN OLD ALARM IN THE HOUR OF VICTORY, BUXTON GOES TO THE INVALID LIST, AND ALONSO'S HELMET EARNS ITS WAGES

The ward's gravest watch is kept in Chicago, where Elly De La Cruz — two hits to his credit in Cincinnati's win — was lifted before the seventh with tightness in the left quadriceps, the selfsame muscle that hobbled his 2025 for months. "I don't think it's very bad," offered the manager Francona, who confessed to double-teaming his shortstop into leaving, "but we need to get him looked at." The examination comes today. In Minnesota, Byron Buxton's right hip — whose alarm this ward has sounded since the spring — has at last claimed him: the center fielder goes to the ten-day invalid list with an impingement, dated back to the seven-and-twentieth. In Sacramento, the Baltimores drew a collective breath when Pete Alonso took a fastball of 94.6 miles to the hour upon the brim of his helmet in the eighth; the slugger went down, rose, and took his base under his own power. "Pete was fine, came out fine," reported the manager Albernaz. "He was typical Pete in the dugout." And in the Bronx, Aaron Judge packs a suitcase: the captain travels with his club on its western swing to ramp up his activities — on-field batting practice among them — with a September return from the rib fracture still the ambition, though likely not upon this trip. "I'm sure it will be ramped up and a lot more involved," said the manager Boone. The Cardinals' rookie Wetherholt, whose Rookie of the Year candidacy these pages weighed only yesterday, goes to the ten-day list with tendinitis of the right wrist.

THE RESTORATION DESK: THE SEPTEMBER GATES SWING INWARD — ANTHONY AND STORY REJOIN THE BOSTON RANKS, MARTE RETURNS TO THE DESERT THIS VERY EVENING, AND SMITH TO THE CHAMPIONS TUESDAY

On the eve of September's expanded rosters, the invalid lists are giving men back. Boston activated Roman Anthony and Trevor Story from the sixty-day rolls on Sunday, and both announced themselves directly, each doubling in the Bronx defeat the card below records. In Arizona, Ketel Marte's ten-day term expires today, and the club intends him in the ranks for this evening's engagement with Philadelphia at Chase Field — the final chapter, the Diamondbacks devoutly hope, of the saga that began when their second baseman failed to appear at Fenway Park on the seventeenth of August. The manager Lovullo, who has received the man's private apology, holds that a public one would serve: "He doesn't know how powerful that would be if he did something like that." And the champions expect their catcher back Tuesday: Will Smith, three months idled by an inflamed disc in the neck, is to be activated when Los Angeles opens its homestand against St. Louis, his rehabilitation assignment complete. "The experience, the calmness in the box, the managing of the pitching staff — all that stuff is crucial," his manager Roberts has said of what returns with him.

THE PROTOCOL DESK: THE CORRESPONDENCE WITH THE NATIONAL'S WEST ACQUIRES A SAN DIEGO CHAPTER — TATIS SURRENDERS HIS ARMOR PIECE BY PIECE

The lively correspondence between the umpiring estate and the National League's western clubs — a week's running feature in these pages, from Vitello's ejections to Webb's first to Wotus dispatched at the lineup-card exchange — has now enrolled the Padres. In the seventh inning at Tropicana Field on Sunday, Fernando Tatis Jr. laid down a bunt, reached when the reliever Booser threw wildly, and sprinted to second — whereupon the first-base umpire Blaser ruled him out for having run too far inside the first-base line, and the base hit was unwritten. The manager Stammen sprang from the dugout and was ejected by the crew chief Fletcher; Tatis followed him to the showers, pausing to strip off his protective armor piece by piece and slam each to the ground for emphasis. "It's a rule made for somebody who hasn't played the game," the right fielder testified afterward. "I just got a base hit taken away from a really tough series. They didn't care to explain. I felt like I played this game for a very long time and I should deserve some answers." Stammen's brief was more lawyerly: "If you're running at the base straight-on and the throw doesn't touch you, it didn't really affect the play." The Herald, noting that the rule in question predates every man on the field, forwards the correspondence to the league offices without further comment.

THE SANDLOT DESK: CURAÇAO TAKES ITS SECOND WORLD TITLE OF THE LITTLE LEAGUES, AND A NEVADA GIRL WRITES A LINE OF HISTORY IN THE LOSING CAUSE

From Williamsport comes word that the boys of Pariba Little League of Willemstad, Curaçao, are champions of the Little League World Series, eleven runs to two over Paseo Verde of Henderson, Nevada — the island's second title, and its first since the 2004 nine that sent Jurickson Profar and Jonathan Schoop on to the big leagues. Down two runs early, the islanders answered with De Lanoi's two-run single, Martina's run-scoring double, and a four-run fifth crowned by De Windt's bases-loaded double, while their pitching trio scattered five hits. The Herald tips its cap besides to the vanquished: Nevada's outfielder Carsynn Meyer became the first American girl ever to play in a Little League World Series title game, and but the second of any nation, following Japan's Sayaka Tsushima in 1998. Tiny island, big bats — and a big footnote for the annals.

The Rest of the Card

A DISPUTED TRAP, A FIVE-RUN FIFTH, AND THE SEASON'S SERIES GOES TO THE PINSTRIPES: YANKEES 16, RED SOX 1

The rubber match this paper flagged yesterday morning turned on a half-second in the right-center gap: Rafaela's diving try in the fifth was ruled a trap, the Crimson Hose lost their challenge — "I didn't even have to watch it. I know I made the catch," the aggrieved center fielder insisted — and the Pinstripes poured five runs through the opened door, Heliot Ramos's three-run blast, his first in New York flannels, leading the flood. The rout ran on from there: Austin Wells struck two homers and drove in five, Goldschmidt added his eighteenth among three runs batted in, Caballero a three-run shot of his own, and Chisholm stole twice more to reach forty, the American's best figure, while Warren carried the ball into the eighth for his ninth victory. The freight matters more than the tonnage: New York takes the season's series from Boston seven games to six — the very October tiebreaker yesterday's number weighed — and holds the top wild-card chair by four games, the tiebreaker in its pocket besides. Anthony's and Story's returns were Boston's chief consolation, as the restoration desk relates.

ONE HIT, TEN STRIKEOUTS, AND HISTORY IN THE BARGAIN: JAYS 7, MARINERS 0

The elder Scherzer's afternoon — seven innings, Raleigh's fourth-inning double the only hit against him, one walk, ten strikeouts, and ninth place all-time seized from Gaylord Perry, as the milestone desk sings above — would have carried the day unassisted, but the Canadians supplied ornament anyway: Kirk's two-run homer in the first, Okamoto's eight-and-twentieth, Guerrero's run-scoring double, and Giménez's two-run single in the eighth. Three straight now for Toronto, a game and a half from Cleveland's wild-card chair; the Seattle nine, blanked and four times beaten running, limp to Boston for this evening's engagement.

HENDERSON STRIKES TWO HOMERS AND A TRIPLE, AND SEVEN UNANSWERED RUNS FINISH THE SWEEP: BALTIMORES 8, ELEPHANTS 5

Down five runs to one by the third in Sacramento, the Baltimores were carried home on Gunnar Henderson's back: a leadoff homer in the first, an infield single, a three-run blast to the right-field berm in the fifth that took the lead for keeps, and an opposite-field run-scoring triple in the eighth — four hits in four trips, two homers, five driven in, with a pair of rally-killing gems at shortstop besides. "It was an outstanding all-around game for Gunnar," ruled the manager Albernaz, and the shortstop, whose summer has run below his own high standard, credited a rare Friday's rest: "It was nice to have nothing to really think about." Mayo's three-run homer in the fourth had begun the seven-unanswered procession; Bassitt took the win, Cano the save, and the sweep of the Elephants leaves the O's — three straight victories, seven of ten — a single game from Cleveland's last chair. Alonso's helmet is the ward's business above; tonight the swing continues at Colorado.

RAMÍREZ RETURNS TO THE FENCE-CLEARING TRADE, AND THE SWEEP IS DECLINED WITH EMPHASIS: GUARDIANS 11, ROYALS 1

Twice beaten in the set and facing the broom, the Forest City nine administered an eleven-to-one correction: José Ramírez homered — his first since June, of which drought the milestone desk has the fuller account — among four runs batted in, Nathaniel Lowe drove home three with his fifteenth, the rookie DeLauter doubled twice, and Adell added three runs batted in of his own while the young Messick held Kansas City to a single run across six innings for his eleventh victory. The Kansas City nine's astonishing surge, chronicled in these pages all week, thus settles at twelve victories in fourteen games; Cleveland's grip on the American's final wild-card chair is one game over Baltimore, a game and a half over Toronto — and the Canadians themselves call at Progressive Field beginning Tuesday.

ACUÑA LEADS OFF THE TENTH, OLSON ENDS IT, AND SEVEN STRAIGHT RIDE THE BROOM: BRAVES 3, ROCKIES 2, TEN INNINGS

The Tomahawk nine made harder work of the Coloradans than the tables suggested they might — Murphy's homer, his second inside four days, and Acuña's run-scoring single built a two-run lead, McCarthy's fourteenth and Norby's eighth-inning single clawed it level — but the tenth restored the natural order: Acuña singled leading off, and Matt Olson lined the walk-off knock to right, Atlanta's seventh consecutive victory and a sweep to close a spotless six-game homestand that began by sweeping the champions themselves. "We're worlds apart from where we were a week ago," said the manager Weiss, whose club at two-and-eighty wins stands dead level with Los Angeles for the National's second first-round bye. The schedule grants no breath: San Francisco calls this very evening at 6:05 for a makeup engagement, Molina opposing Elder.

CROW-ARMSTRONG STRIKES TWO MORE, BUT BURNS AND THE ROOKIE STEWART CARRY THE NIGHT: REDS 7, CUBS 5

The order Sosa placed Saturday, this paper's lead of yesterday, has swollen beyond the grocer's arithmetic: Pete Crow-Armstrong opened Sunday night with a leadoff blast off Burns's fastball of 98.9 miles to the hour and closed it with a ninth-inning shot off Pagán — five homers in two games, a feat managed by Swanson at the turn of this very July, and before him by no Cub since Kingman in 1979 and Billy Williams in 1968 — his August count of fourteen the most in a month by any man of four-and-twenty years or fewer since Griffey the younger in May of 1994. The Bruins lost anyway, and therein the rub: Chase Burns pitched to his fifteenth victory against three defeats, the rookie Sal Stewart homered in a third consecutive game — his one-and-thirtieth, his National-leading runs-batted-in count now at one hundred five — and Stephenson, Myers, and the young Rodríguez (three driven in) added blasts of their own. A third straight defeat for Chicago and a third series lost running; the wild-card cushion holds at four and a half, but Milwaukee arrives at Wrigley this very evening, as the desk note appoints. De La Cruz's quadriceps is the ward's worry above.

DURAN SUPPLIES A HOMER AND A GROUND-RULE DOUBLE, AND THE GAME'S BEST RECORD TAKES ONE ON THE CHIN: RANGERS 7, BREWERS 4

The Texas nine spotted Milwaukee two first-inning runs and then ran off seven unanswered: Ezequiel Duran's fifteenth homer leveled the account, his two-run ground-rule double took the lead in the fifth, and Pederson's four-and-twentieth added margin before Burger and Freeman singled home the sixth and seventh — three runs batted in for Duran, whose "energetic spark," as the wires put it, has become the Arlington offense's signature. Sánchez's two-run homer in the seventh trimmed the account for the Milwaukees, whose four-game winning streak dies at five-and-eighty wins against two-and-fifty defeats — still the game's best ledger by a distance. Alexander took the decision, Latz his seven-and-twentieth save; Texas, two games from Houston's crown and two from the wild-card row, hosts the Elephants tonight while the Brewers proceed to Wrigley and the appointment below.

PEÑA OPENS THE SCORING, AND WADE CLOSES THE ARGUMENT FROM THE BENCH: 'STROS 6, METS 3

Jeremy Peña greeted the first pitch of consequence with his seventeenth homer and later singled home a second run, but New York answered through Lindor and Soto, whose first-inning blasts briefly promised a Queens evening of resistance. The sixth settled it: LaMonte Wade Jr., summoned from the bench, struck a go-ahead two-run homer — his third — and Varsho's seventh-inning groundout cashed two more amid a Young throwing error. Pecko took his first victory of the season, Hader sealed his one-and-twentieth save, and the Houston nine depart New York with two series claimed on the excursion — the Pinstripes' scalp among them — their crown in the West two games clear of Texas. The Flushing nine, six-and-seventy times beaten, greet Tampa Bay tonight.

TWO INCHES OF GLOVE, ONE RUN ALLOWED, AND THE SWEEP OF THE SERAPHS IS SIGNED: PHILLIES 5, ANGELS 2

Zack Wheeler, winless since the twelfth of July, sat down with his counselors this week and found the culprit in a graph: his glove hand had sagged two inches. Restored to proper altitude, he held Anaheim to a single run across six innings — his first turn of six full since late July — while Realmuto and Sosa supplied homers, the latter's seventh taking the lead for good in the seventh inning, and Harper doubled home the fifth run past a failed Angel challenge. "Just bring the front arm up a little bit and go from there," the ace shrugged. Kerkering sealed it, the sweep makes four straight for Philadelphia, and the Anaheim nine have now dropped seven running. Tonight the Philadelphias call in the desert, where Marte returns — the restoration desk above has the delicacies.

GLASNOW CARRIES THE FINALE ALONE, AND TEOSCAR SUPPLIES THE THUNDER: DODGERS 6, TIGERS 1

The assignment that fell to Tyler Glasnow when the unicorn's Sunday was scratched — as yesterday's ward recorded — was discharged without incident: the right-hander ran his ledger to four victories without defeat, and Teoscar Hernández, robbed of a homer in this very yard on Saturday by Báez's basket catch, settled accounts with a two-run blast in the sixth among his two runs batted in. Muncy singled home an insurance run, Betts and Freeman doubled, and the Angelenos took the series from the Bengals two games to one, McGonigle's run-scoring single the home nine's whole account. At two-and-eighty wins the champions remain level with Atlanta for the second bye; Smith's Tuesday return, and the roster's September reinforcements, are the restoration desk's business above.

VALDEZ AND TRIOLO CLEAR THE FENCES, AND BURLESON'S HUNDREDTH ARRIVES IN A LOSING CAUSE: PIRATES 5, CARDINALS 4

The Buccaneers built their lead on Esmerlyn Valdez's two-run homer, his sixteenth, and Triolo's third, and then survived a St. Louis reply that came in waves — Herrera driving home two, and Alec Burleson singling home the run that brought his season's account to precisely one hundred runs batted in, the century this paper saw him standing one shy of on Friday morning. Ashcraft pitched to his fourteenth victory against five defeats, among the National's best figures, and Montgomery held the ninth for his seventh save. Two straight for Pittsburgh; the Mound City nine, twice beaten running and five games from the last chair, lose Wetherholt to the ward above besides.

KEASCHALL PUNCTUATES, MATTHEWS PROSECUTES, AND THE MINNESOTANS TAKE THE FINALE: TWINS 5, WHITE SOX 1

Matthews pitched deep into the evening for his ninth victory, the Central's leaders held scoreless until the ninth, while the Minnesota attack did its business early — Bell singling home two among his pair of runs batted in, Larnach doubling home two more in the first, and Keaschall's ninth homer supplying the seventh-inning punctuation. The White Stockings' account was Montgomery's ninth-inning single; their grip on the Central nonetheless holds at three games and a half over Cleveland, and they proceed to Houston for this evening's meeting of division leaders. Minnesota, Buxton-less as the ward relates, hosts Detroit tonight.

EIGHT INNINGS OF SILENCE, THEN SIX RUNS AT THE STROKE OF NINE: MARLINS 6, NATIONALS 2

The Miami nine carried a blank scorecard into the ninth inning at Washington, two runs in arrears to Nuñez's double and Lile's sacrifice fly, and then produced the entire evening's offense in a single frame: Marsee struck by a pitch with the bases loaded, Mack's sacrifice fly worth two runs by the grace of Pinckney's throwing error, and Otto Lopez's tenth homer to crown the six-run outburst. Fulton collected his first victory, the Washingtons' late-inning arithmetic collapsed entire, and the Fish — three games and a half from the National's last chair — renew the quarrel on the same grounds this evening at 6:45.

The tables on August's final morning, surveyed once around. In the American: Tampa Bay's lead in the East is four games and a half over New York, whose season's-series tiebreaker over Boston is now banked; the White Sox hold the Central by three and a half over Cleveland; Houston keeps the West by two over Texas; and the wild-card row reads New York, Boston, and Cleveland's last chair by one game over Baltimore, a game and a half over Toronto, and two over Texas. In the National: Atlanta by five in the East, Milwaukee by eight in the Central, Los Angeles by nine and a half in the West — and the second bye remains a dead heat, Atlanta and the champions locked at two-and-eighty wins apiece for a second consecutive morning. In the wild-card row the Cubs and Phillies share the top chairs at seven-and-seventy wins, Arizona holds the last with San Diego half a game astern, Miami three and a half back, and St. Louis five. Tonight's card runs to twelve engagements, all verified against the schedule, and the desk directs the reader's eye to three: at 6:05 the Giants call at Atlanta for a makeup engagement, Molina opposing Elder; at 7:40 the appointment yesterday's number twice made comes due at Wrigley Field, where Milwaukee and Chicago — first and second in the Central, eight games between them — open four straight, Harrison opposing Holmes; and at 9:40 the Phillies open in the desert, where Marte's return is the restoration desk's story above. The Yankees, with their traveling captain, open at Anaheim at 9:38; and when the morrow comes it brings September, the eight-and-twenty-man rosters, and a regular season with its final day — the seven-and-twentieth of that month — at last in distant view. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: SOSA ASKS FOR THREE IN THE CAGE, AND CROW-ARMSTRONG FILLS THE ORDER TO THE LETTER: CUBS 17, REDLEGS 5
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 53 · Sunday, the Thirtieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 17 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

SOSA ASKS FOR THREE IN THE CAGE, AND CROW-ARMSTRONG FILLS THE ORDER TO THE LETTER: CUBS 17, REDLEGS 5

On a Wrigley afternoon thick with the club's own legends, Sammy Sosa places a request of the young center fielder — 'I want three out of you today' — and Pete Crow-Armstrong obliges precisely: homers in the first, the second, and the seventh, four hits in six trips, six runs batted in, and a first career three-homer game that lifts his season's worth, by the modern reckonings, above every Cub summer since Sosa's own — while the Reds are reduced by the eighth inning to pitching their catcher

Down in the batting cage beneath Wrigley Field on Saturday, before a pitch had been thrown, Sammy Sosa placed an order. "He was like, 'I want three out of you today. I need three,'" Pete Crow-Armstrong reported afterward, and the young man confessed that the audience unsettled him more than any pitcher has lately managed: "There were legends on legends down in the cage before the game. If anything, the most intimidating part of today was doing my pregame routine in front of Sammy Sosa and Billy Williams." Whereupon he went out and filled the order like a grocer's boy. A leadoff blast off the left-hander Abbott's fastball to open the home first — his four-and-thirtieth. A curveball ripped off the right-field pole an inning later for two more — five-and-thirty. And in the seventh, with the count of the afternoon long since settled, a three-run drive to left-center off Santillan for six-and-thirty, the first three-homer game of his major-league life, four hits in six trips, six runs batted in, and thirteen total bases as the Cubs buried Cincinnati seventeen runs to five.

The arithmetic desk begs leave to place the afternoon in its proper cabinet. It was Crow-Armstrong's fifth game this season of ten total bases or better — a count matched since 1900 only by Larry Walker, Johnny Mize, and Jimmie Foxx, with Nelson Cruz's six standing alone above — and by the FanGraphs reckoning his season's worth now stands at 9.1 wins above the replacement standard, a figure exceeded in all the Cubs' annals only by Hornsby's 1929, Sosa's own 2001, Banks's 1959, and Santo's 1967. The company, in short, is the pantheon, and the man keeping it is a center fielder of four-and-twenty who also holds two-and-thirty stolen bases. Asked to adjudicate the Most Valuable question, his teammate Bregman declined the pretense of suspense: "I think everyone here knows what we think about Pete's season." The reader will find in the ward below the morning's other entry in that argument — the two-time laureate Ohtani's mound return, postponed anew the selfsame day.

Nor did the master carry the freight alone: the Cubs struck nineteen hits, Suzuki three of them with his three-and-twentieth homer, Bregman three more with his twentieth, the catcher Carson Kelly a three-run blast among four driven in, and Taylor four hits besides, while Abbott was excused after three innings bearing seven runs. By the eighth the Queen City's bullpen ledger had run so far into the red that the catcher Trevino was handed the ball — the position player's inning yielding Kelly's double and Suzuki's homer among four hits, which the Herald records without cruelty, the practice being lately epidemic. Cincinnati's consolations were genuine if outnumbered: Sal Stewart's thirtieth homer and Suárez's twentieth — the milestone desk below sings the rookie's fuller glory. So dies a three-game Chicago skid, as this paper noted it running; the North Siders stand seven-and-seventy wins against nine-and-fifty defeats, eight astern of Milwaukee with the wild-card's first chair still five games safe, and the set concludes this evening at 7:20 by the Eastern clock, Burns and his fourteen-and-three opposing Imanaga.

News Around the League

THE INFIRMARY WARD: THE UNICORN'S GATE, HALF-OPEN ONLY YESTERDAY, SWINGS SHUT AGAIN — WHILE RENGIFO LEAVES BY CART AND CAVALLI BY COMEBACKER

The appointment this ward held open only yesterday morning is canceled. Shohei Ohtani will not take the mound in this afternoon's Detroit finale, his manager Roberts confirmed Saturday, and the timetable for his return to pitching is now frankly indefinite: the two-way marvel reported that he did not feel his best after Friday's abbreviated bullpen session, the left knee's old soreness having resurfaced in company with the right biceps and, in the manager's accounting, the "overall body." "If any pitcher was feeling like this," Roberts said, "we wouldn't run him out there" — and more candidly still: "To be quite frank, I just don't see everything getting to 100% by the end of the season. But there's a lot of pitchers that are not 100% and still viable." The club will determine the next steps upon returning to Los Angeles on the first of September; Glasnow, who was appointed to pitch this afternoon in any arrangement, now carries the whole of it. Ohtani's ledger when the knee first closed the gate on the third of July: eight-and-two, with an earned-run figure of 1.79 across fourteen starts.

The ward's other beds filled quickly. In Tampa Bay, the Padres' Rengifo was carried from the field by cart, his knee the complaint by the wires' account, on an evening already unkind to him, as the card below relates. In Washington, the Nationals' starter Cavalli departed his engagement with Miami when a comebacker struck his right ankle. And in the Bronx, the rookie shortstop Lombard — whose sorrows at shortstop this paper chronicled only Thursday — left the nightcap with discomfort of the right knee, though the first imaging read kindly and his manager Boone pronounced it "a day to day situation."

THE DEALINGS DESK: THE METS SET ROBERT UPON THE WAIVER WIRE AS THE SEPTEMBER BELL NEARS, AND KELENIC TAKES ANOTHER SWING AT NEW YORK

The waiver wire, lately the busiest thoroughfare in the game, has received another passenger of quality. The Mets have placed the outfielder Luis Robert Jr. upon it, by the account of a source — the club itself declining to confirm — offering any of the other nine-and-twenty clubs the chance to claim him and assume the remainder of his wages: some three millions of this season's salary and a two-million buyout of next year's twenty-million option, which New York is thought unlikely to exercise. The irony is that the merchandise has rarely shown better: unwanted at the August deadline fresh off a spinal complaint, Robert has since batted .311 with six homers across nineteen games and learned left field besides. The calendar explains the timing — a man must be in his organization before the first of September to be eligible for October's wars — and the Herald notes that the wire has been no thoroughfare of commerce lately: Suárez and Friedl, whose placement these pages recorded Wednesday, both passed through unclaimed. Elsewhere the transactions column records a homecoming of sorts: Jarred Kelenic, seven-and-twenty years of age and taken sixth overall by the Mets in the draft of 2018 before his wanderings began, has signed a minor-league engagement with the Yankees and reports to their Scranton garrison.

THE MILESTONE DESK: STEWART STANDS ALONE AMONG REDS FRESHMEN AT THIRTY AND ONE HUNDRED, CHOURIO BANKS HIS THIRD TWENTY BEFORE AGE THREE-AND-TWENTY, AND SÁNCHEZ RINGS UP TWO HUNDRED AGAIN

Three entries for the ledger of accomplishment. In Chicago, Sal Stewart's thirtieth homer — struck amid Saturday's general bombardment, as the lead column relates — made him the first rookie in all the Cincinnati club's history to pair thirty homers with a hundred runs batted in, his total standing at one hundred four atop the entire National; the researchers note that should he finish master of all baseball's table, only Ted Williams in 1939 and Dropo in 1950 managed the feat as freshmen, and that his Rookie of the Year argument against the Cardinal Wetherholt and the Met Benge now carries history in its saddlebags. In Milwaukee, Jackson Chourio opened Saturday's scoring with his twentieth homer — a third consecutive season of twenty though he stands but two-and-twenty years of age, a distinction owned by only seventeen men ever, half the prior sixteen now enshrined at Cooperstown: Ott, Williams, Mathews, Mantle, Kaline, Robinson, Cepeda, and Griffey the younger. And in Anaheim, the Phillies' Cristopher Sánchez struck out the side in the fifth to reach two hundred strikeouts for a second consecutive summer, then declined to linger over it: "I'm proud of back-to-back 200-strikeout seasons, but we just have to keep going." His stated ambitions — a Series, a Cy Young, the club's first twenty-game winner since Halladay in 2010 — the desk records as entirely plausible.

THE VALEDICTORY DESK: KENT'S NUMBER ASCENDS BY THE BAY, AND BONDS SUPPLIES THE EMBRACE — AND THE SHAKE — OF OLD

Before the nightcap by the Bay on Saturday, the Giants raised Jeff Kent's No. 21 to the rafters of Oracle Park, making the new Hall of Famer the sixteenth of that franchise so honored, with Marichal, Baker, Posey, and Will Clark among the receiving line. The exchange the house had waited for came from Barry Bonds: the two old teammates, whose frost in shared flannels was the stuff of a thousand columns, embraced — and then, to general laughter, reenacted their famous dugout scuffle of 2002, Bonds seizing Kent and shaking him with theatrical relish. "He and I have never gone out to dinner, but I'll go to war with that guy any day of the week," Kent testified. "If Bonds and I weren't fighting in the dugout, we wouldn't have what we've got." The honoree, elected to Cooperstown by the Contemporary Era committee, turned advocate on the spot — "Barry, keep with it brother, you've got a shot, man" — and sentimentalist besides, for his son Kaeden, three-and-twenty and lately acquired into the Giants' system in the Ramos trade, homered twice for their Eugene farmhands on Thursday. The home nine, as the card relates, honored the day by winning the game that followed.

THE PROTOCOL DESK: THE CORRESPONDENCE EXTENDS TO THE LINEUP CARDS — WOTUS IS EJECTED BEFORE A PITCH IS THROWN

The lively correspondence between the umpiring estate and the National's West, remarked in yesterday's number, has now reached the pregame formalities. Ron Wotus, senior counselor to the San Francisco baseball operation, was ejected from Saturday's opening game during the exchange of lineup cards — before a single pitch had been thrown — the crew chief Porter having declined to continue a conversation Wotus wished to prolong regarding Friday evening's disputed calls: the strike-three-that-wasn't to Nootbaar, uncontested by the home catcher, and the fair-ball ruling that fattened Arizona's five-run third. "At one point, he didn't want to discuss it anymore, and I did," Wotus explained with admirable economy. "I was ejected, so that's what it was about." The desk's running tally for the week by the Bay: the manager Vitello twice, the ace Webb once, and now a senior counselor dispatched at home plate with the lineup cards still in hand — a completeness of representation the Herald can only admire.

The Rest of the Card

THE ROOKIE BENNETT SILENCES THE BRONX, AND THE NINTH ADDS THE FLOURISH: HUB NINE 6, BRONX BOMBERS 0

The daylight half of the separate-admission twin bill belonged entirely to Jake Bennett, the rookie left-hander, who fired six scoreless innings on three hits with seven strikeouts and not a walk, nine-and-fifty of his three-and-eighty pitches finding the zone. "He was the Bennett we're used to seeing," ruled the interim manager Tracy. Abreu's three-and-twentieth homer opened the scoring in the first, Rutschman collected three hits, and the ninth added four — Monasterio's two-run single the heaviest freight — while Rodón absorbed the loss. The evening's answer, and the rubber match's stakes, follow directly below.

FRIED RETURNS ON SIXTY-THREE PITCHES, AND THIRTEEN SINGLES CARRY THE NIGHTCAP: BRONX BOMBERS 9, HUB NINE 2

The appointment yesterday's desk note recorded was kept: Max Fried, restored from his elbow's bone bruise, took the evening half and gave the Yankees three innings and two-thirds of encouragement on three-and-sixty pitches. "It was nice to get back out there and get the competitive juices flowing," said the left-hander, and his mates did the rest by the humblest means imaginable — thirteen singles, nary a homer, every post in the batting order scoring a run, five of them crossing in the eighth, with Rice driving home three. Sogard's third homer was Boston's account; Blackburn took the decision, and Lombard's knee is the ward's business above. The split leaves the ancient rivals level at six victories apiece on the season, and this afternoon's rubber at 1:35 — Suarez opposing Warren — settles a series that may yet decide an October tiebreaker. New York's grip on the top wild-card chair stands at three games over Boston.

THE HISS, THE BASKET CATCH, AND A SINGLE THAT BOUNCED ITS WAY TO GLORY: DETROITS 2, BOYS IN BLUE 1

The ninth inning at Comerica Park was Javier Báez's private theater. First the glove: Teoscar Hernández's drive to left-center — a homer in eleven parks, by the trackers' certification — sent young Clark sprinting 122 feet from center until he heard the hiss by which Detroit's outfielders announce themselves, and Báez, having covered 112 feet of his own from left, took it in a basket at the warning track, catching his snapped necklace with the other hand. "The ball's more important in that moment," he allowed. "But I have both." Then the bat: a leadoff double in the home half off Dreyer, a sacrifice from Clark, two walks to fill the bases, and McGonigle — hitless in sixteen trips — lofting a ball that struck the ground and bounded over the left-field fence, a walk-off single by ground rule, of all the endings the pastime keeps in its coat. Báez had scored Detroit's first run too, aboard for Torres's double in the third; Jansen took the victory against his old employers, Snell's six innings going unrewarded. The champions thus stand level with Atlanta at one-and-eighty wins and five-and-fifty defeats in the contest for the National's second bye — and this afternoon's finale, as the ward relates, belongs to Glasnow alone.

TATIS STEALS HOME, AND TAMPA BAY STEALS THE GAME BACK: GULF COAST CLUB 7, MISSION NINE 6

San Diego assembled a six-to-three lead by the seventh with genuine panache — Tatis stealing home outright, France striking his nineteenth homer, Machado driving in two — and then watched four runs undo it in the home half: Yandy Díaz's three-run single, abetted by Rengifo's errant throw, and the fleet Simpson slapping the go-ahead single before roaring at his own dugout, a display from the quietest man in the room. "Just kind of blacked out right there," he grinned. Caminero's six-and-thirtieth homer — now a single blast behind Alvarez's American lead — and Aranda's seventeenth had kept the hosts within reach; Baker sealed his nine-and-thirtieth save, and the league leaders' three-and-thirtieth comeback victory of the season, their one-and-eightieth overall, stretches the East to four games and a half over New York. The set concludes at 1:40 this afternoon, Ray opposing Rasmussen; Rengifo's cart is the ward's sadder business.

BENINTENDI SUPPLIES THE FIRST RUN AND THE LAST WORD, AND JENKINS OPENS HIS ACCOUNT: SOUTH SIDERS 3, NORTH STARS 2

Andrew Benintendi singled home the game's first run and settled its verdict with a sixth-inning homer, his fourteenth, while between his contributions the young Walker Jenkins — whose debut these pages attended Friday — drove home the first run of his major-league life by force-out in the second. Fedde took the decision, Hudson his seventh save, and the White Sox have won four running, their grip on the Central now four games and a half over Cleveland, whose own Saturday sorrows appear below.

LOWE OPENS THE LEDGER, FLORES CLEARS THE BASES' WORTH: SMOKY CITY NINE 6, CARDS 2

Brandon Lowe greeted the afternoon with a leadoff homer, his eight-and-twentieth, and the fifth inning settled matters when Rafael Flores Jr. struck a three-run blast, his seventh, with Gonzales's run-scoring double closing the accounts in the ninth. Mlodzinski pitched to his seventh victory; the young Báez's fifth homer was St. Louis's brightest moment on an afternoon that dropped the Redbirds four games and a half from the National's last chair, their obligations now running chiefly to the arithmetic of other clubs' defeats.

TWO RUNS DELIVERED ON A SINGLE BALL FOUR: TORONTOS 4, PUGET SOUND MEN 3

Seattle banked a three-run lead behind Raleigh's nineteenth homer and Ward's two-run single, and surrendered it by increments of carelessness: in the fifth, Springer's bases-loaded walk became a two-run transaction when Bazardo's fourth ball skipped past the catcher and Bateman came scampering home from second; in the sixth, Bateman singled the account level and Kirk singled it ahead, and there it stayed. Soriano collected the win, Varland his one-and-thirtieth save, and the Torontos — two straight now — sit a game and a half from Cleveland's wild-card chair, of which more below.

KELLY THROWS SEVEN CLEAN, AND NOOTBAAR'S SLAM FINDS THE COVE: D-BACKS 7, FRISCO NINE 1

The daylight half by the Bay went entirely to Arizona: Merrill Kelly pitched seven shutout innings, and Lars Nootbaar — Friday's leadoff-homer hero in these pages — emerged from the bench in the seventh to strike a pinch-hit grand slam that cleared the right-field arcade and found the waters of McCovey Cove, the first Arizona man to bathe a ball there since Varsho in September of 2020. "The guys in front of me did a good job of loading the bases," the modest author explained. The victory draws the D-backs dead level with idle-no-more San Diego for the National's final chair; the pregame ejection is the protocol desk's business above.

ON THE DAY OF KENT'S NUMBER, ELDRIDGE COLLECTS FOUR AND THE HONORS ARE DIVIDED: FRISCO NINE 7, D-BACKS 2

The nightcap answered the matinee: with Kent's one-and-twenty fresh upon the wall, the young Eldridge drove home four runs on three singles, Devers added two more among his own three knocks, and Sanmartin pitched to the victory as San Francisco took the evening game seven runs to two and split the day's labors. Vargas drove in a pair for the visitors, whose gains of the afternoon were thus half returned by nightfall — the last chair shared this morning, as the card above relates.

CREWS BOOKENDS THE AFTERNOON AND SETTLES THE TENTH: CAPITAL NINE 5, FLORIDIANS 4

Dylan Crews opened Washington's account with a two-run single in the third — the catcher Mack's errant throw compounding the damage as House and Vivas followed with blows of their own — and closed it in the tenth, singling home Nuñez for the walk-off after Miami had clawed level, Stowers's two-run double and Heriberto Hernández's tying two-run homer, his two-and-twentieth, doing the visitors' work in the seventh. Ribalta took the win, and the Capital nine have three straight; the Fish, four games from the National's last chair, must resume the argument at 12:15 this very afternoon on the same grounds.

PÉREZ HOLDS THE LINE, AND DUBÓN RUNS THROUGH THE STOP SIGN: ATLANTA 2, MOUNTAIN MEN 1

Colorado led by Castro's sixth-inning single until the eighth, when the Braves assembled a two-out rally of singles by Olson and Dubón and Michael Harris II's sharp double to left — Dubón running clean through his coach's stop sign at third and scoring at a stroll when the throw went to second. Martín Pérez supplied five and two-thirds sturdy innings, Suter took the decision, and Fuentes sealed his third save. Six straight victories now for Atlanta, whose one-and-eighty wins stand level with Los Angeles this morning in the contest for the National's second bye — an appointment of arithmetic the desk note weighs below.

TWO HOURS OFF THE INVALID LIST, SOTO RIPS THE GO-AHEAD: METROPOLITANS 6, HOUSTON NINE 2

Juan Soto, restored Saturday from five weeks' exile with a strained left calf, fouled a pitch off his leg in the fifth, hopped about while "everything went through my mind," then stepped back in and lined the go-ahead single to right at a hundred miles to the hour. "He's right up there with the absolute best hitters on the planet," observed the interim manager Green, "so it's unsurprising that he finds his timing quicker than the rest of us do." Jared Young drove home three, the triple among his blows, and McLean pitched to his tenth victory; Yordan Alvarez's seven-and-thirtieth homer, stretching his league-leading runs-batted-in count to three-and-ninety, was the visitors' principal reply. Houston departs Queens holding the West by two games over Texas — both beaten Saturday — while the Mets bank a second straight.

A TWELFTH VICTORY IN THIRTEEN GAMES, AND ROJAS DRIVES HOME FOUR: MISSOURIANS 8, GUARDIANS 3

Cleveland led early on Angel Martínez's two-run homer and was buried methodically thereafter: Collins's two-run double in the fifth, Perez's go-ahead double in the sixth ahead of a four-run outburst fattened by Ramírez's error, and Josh Rojas — a two-run single in the sixth, a two-run homer in the eighth — accounting for four runs batted in altogether. Gose collected his first victory, and the Kansas City surge this paper has chronicled all week runs now to twelve victories in thirteen games. Cleveland's hold on the American's last wild-card chair is a single game over Baltimore with Toronto a game and a half astern, and the set concludes at 1:40 this afternoon, Lugo opposing Messick.

CHOURIO OPENS HIS THIRD TWENTY-HOMER LEDGER, AND THE BEST RECORD ROLLS ALONG: CREAM CITY NINE 5, ARLINGTON MEN 3

Jackson Chourio's twentieth homer opened the scoring — the milestone desk above has the marvel of his youth — and Contreras added his thirteenth as Milwaukee dispatched Texas for a fourth consecutive victory, Drohan pitching to the decision and Megill sealing his five-and-twentieth save. Nimmo's fourteenth homer and Freeman's first were the visitors' account. The Brewers stand five-and-eighty wins against one-and-fifty defeats, the game's best ledger by a comfortable margin — and Monday evening they call at Wrigley Field, where the Central's top two meet with eight games between them.

THE BULLPEN BENDS FOUR TIMES AND BREAKS NOT ONCE: BIRDS 5, WHITE ELEPHANTS 3

Baltimore's relief corps spent the final four innings escorting baserunners off the premises: Hoppe pitched out of a bases-filled sixth, and in the seventh Yennier Cano, summoned with the sacks loaded and one out, froze into his statuary pose after striking out Gelof and Butler back to back on splitters. "That was electric, and we needed it," ruled the manager Albernaz. Cowser's thirteenth homer led the offense, Baz took the win, and Kittredge sealed his eighth save; two straight now for the O's on their western swing, a single game from Cleveland's chair — an arithmetic growing warmer by the morning, as the card above attests.

TEN INNINGS IN ANAHEIM, AND TURNER CASHES THE EXTRA FRAME: QUAKERS 4, SERAPHS 2

Marsh's early run-scoring single held until Neto's three-and-twentieth homer leveled the account in the eighth, whereupon the tenth settled it: Schwarber doubled home Realmuto on a drive that glanced off two Angel gloves, and Trea Turner singled home two more. Duran took the decision, and Sánchez's two-hundredth strikeout — the milestone desk's business above — anchored the staff's evening. Twelve victories in fourteen games now for Philadelphia, whose second wild-card chair is four games clear of both San Diego and Arizona.

A Sabbath survey of the tables, taken in one draught. In the American: Tampa Bay's lead in the East is four games and a half over New York, with Boston seven and a half astern and today's Bronx rubber deciding the season's series between them; the White Sox hold the Central by four and a half over Cleveland; Houston keeps the West by two over Texas; and the wild-card row reads New York, Boston, and Cleveland's last chair by a single game over surging Baltimore, a game and a half over Toronto, and two over Texas. In the National: Atlanta by five in the East, Milwaukee by eight in the Central with the game's best record at five-and-eighty wins, and Los Angeles by nine in the West — but mark the second bye, where Atlanta's six straight victories and the champions' Saturday stumble leave the two clubs dead level at one-and-eighty wins apiece; and mark the last chair, where San Diego and Arizona this morning sit in each other's laps, with Miami four back and St. Louis four and a half. Today's card runs to fourteen engagements, all verified against the schedule, opening at 12:15 with the Fish and the Capital nine resuming yesterday's tenth-inning quarrel. The desk directs the reader's eye to the 1:35 hour in the Bronx, Suarez opposing Warren with a possible October tiebreaker in the balance, and to a crowded 1:40: the Royals' twelve-of-thirteen surge concludes its Cleveland business with Lugo opposing Messick, Glasnow carries the Detroit finale alone — the unicorn's postponement being the ward's sorrow above — and Ray opposes Rasmussen at Tampa Bay. The evening belongs to Wrigley at 7:20, Burns and his fourteen-and-three against Imanaga; and Monday the Brewers themselves call at that same yard, where the Central's top two shall have it out. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: THE APPOINTMENT IS KEPT: SKUBAL WEEPS IN THE TUNNEL, THEN FANS SEVEN OF HIS OWN — TROLLEY DODGERS 2, MOTOR CITY NINE 1
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 52 · Saturday, the Nine-and-Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE APPOINTMENT IS KEPT: SKUBAL WEEPS IN THE TUNNEL, THEN FANS SEVEN OF HIS OWN — TROLLEY DODGERS 2, MOTOR CITY NINE 1

Twice this paper marked Friday upon the almanac, and the evening honored the billing: the two-time Cy Young laureate takes the Comerica Park mound for the eight-and-seventieth time of his life and the first in visiting grays, receives a standing ovation and a tribute film, dries his eyes, and holds the club that raised him to one run across six innings — young Clark's triple the only blemish — before Freeman's eighth-inning single settles the verdict

The tears arrived before the first pitch did. Tarik Skubal has pitched at Comerica Park more often than at any yard in the land — seven summers' worth, two Cy Young Awards' worth — and when he walked in from his pregame warmups Friday evening to a standing ovation and a tribute film upon the scoreboard, the eyes gave out before the arm was asked to. "There were definitely tears," he confessed afterward. "Luckily enough, I was able to make it to the tunnel before more happened." This was the reunion the Herald's almanac desk appointed on Thursday and the desk note confirmed only yesterday morning: the late ace of the Detroits, carried west in the blockbuster before the deadline, returned at last to face the club that raised him — for the first time wearing another city's name across his chest.

The sentiment ended at the top of the mound. Skubal struck out seven Tigers without walking a man, scattered four hits across six innings, and was dented only once — and here the pastime showed its taste for symmetry, for the dent was administered by Max Clark, the one-and-twenty-year-old center fielder whose Comerica heroics this paper sang on Wednesday last, who lined a fifth-inning triple past Teoscar Hernández to cash Valencia and put the home nine ahead. The ovations, it must be reported, curdled somewhat as the evening wore along — boos raining down amid what may charitably have been calls of "Skooooob" — and Skubal was unbothered by either currency. "I think I did a good job of keeping baseball baseball," he said. "Obviously, this place is special."

His old mates could not make the run stand. The Trolley Dodgers drew level in the sixth, Rojas singling home Enrique Hernández, and in the eighth Freddie Freeman lined a sharp single to center to cash Teoscar Hernández with the run that decided it. Phillips took the victory in relief, Scott sealed his twentieth save, and a three-game Los Angeles losing streak — administered whole in Atlanta, as these pages chronicled — was put to rest, the champions' hold on the National's West standing at nine games over San Diego this morning. Detroit's Anderson, for his part, walked five in under five innings and escaped unscored upon, which is its own variety of accomplishment. The engagement resumes this very afternoon at 1:10 by the Eastern clock — and Sunday's finale at 1:40 may carry a marvel of its own, of which the infirmary ward below has particulars.

News Around the League

THE COUNTING-HOUSE DESK: THE COUNTY SAYS YES BY FIVE VOTES TO TWO, AND THE RAYS' TWENTY-YEAR WANDERING FINDS ITS FOREVER HOME

The final hurdle this paper flagged only yesterday morning has been cleared at a bound. The Hillsborough County Board of County Commissioners on Friday approved the Rays' agreement for their "Forever Home" ballpark upon Hillsborough College's Dale Mabry campus by a vote of five to two — a more comfortable arithmetic than the city council's four-to-three squeaker of Thursday — and with city and county blessings both in hand, the longest-running stadium serial in the game closes its final chapter. "Forever starts now," pronounced the club's managing partner Zalupski, who eleven months ago, at his ownership group's very first press conference, named a permanent Tampa Bay ballpark his "first and highest priority." There remain the community benefits process and the validation of the bonds before ground is broken, but the two-decade question of where the Tampa Bay enterprise shall live is answered. The Herald notes with satisfaction that the club so housed spent the selfsame evening becoming the first American League nine to reach eighty victories, as the rest of the card relates — a franchise that settled its future and padded its present inside a single Friday.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: OHTANI THROWS HIS TWENTY PITCHES AND EYES SUNDAY'S MOUND, WHILE FRIED RETURNS TO TAKE ONE HALF OF THE BRONX TWIN BILL

The unicorn's gate, so long watched in these pages, may swing open within the week. Shohei Ohtani threw a bullpen session of some twenty pitches at Comerica Park on Friday — lighter than his custom, and by his own choosing — and his manager Roberts allowed that, depending on how the two-way marvel recovers, he could take a big-league mound as soon as Sunday's finale in Detroit, likely for a single inning as a curtain-raiser ahead of Glasnow. "It's not a hiding-the-ball situation," Roberts said, promising a verdict after conferring with his star and the pitching counselor Prior. Ohtani has not pitched since the third of July, his left knee's soreness having idled an arm that had gone eight-and-two with a 1.79 earned-run figure across fourteen starts. The same ward reports the Yankees' Max Fried — shelved by a bone bruise of the left elbow — is to be activated this very day to start one half of the doubleheader against Boston, of which appointment the desk note has more; and in Flushing, the Mets' relief captain Díaz works through a bullpen progression of his own, a rehabilitation assignment still between him and the September wars.

THE VALEDICTORY DESK: ON THE NIGHT ONE CY YOUNG MAN RETURNED TO COMERICA, THE HOUSE HELD HOPE FOR ONE MORE FROM ANOTHER

While Skubal was drying his eyes upon the Comerica mound, the manager Hinch was speaking of the other Cy Young laureate in the building — Justin Verlander, now in the one-and-twentieth year of his major-league life — who has not thrown a pitch in anger since the thirtieth of March, waylaid first by the hip and then by the hamstring, and who announced in July that this season shall be his last. The old lion is now throwing off the slope of the mound, a step shy of a proper bullpen session, and Hinch pronounced him "as encouraged as I've heard him since his injury." "I sense that he is building towards something positive," said the manager, "and that he's going to be able to make at least one appearance." Twice already this season a Comerica homecoming has been scratched by the body's veto, so no date is penciled; but Detroit, which gave Cabrera his long goodbye three summers ago, knows the worth of a proper farewell, and the Herald keeps a column of type set aside against the day.

THE DEBUT DESK: JENKINS COLLECTS HIS FIRST HIT TO A STANDING OVATION — AND THE MAN WHO CAUGHT HIS LOUDEST DRIVE WAS PETERS, WHOSE OWN VIGIL ENDS AT FIVE

Target Field rose to its feet Friday before Walker Jenkins had seen a single major-league pitch — the summons of the Twins' finest prospect having been announced in yesterday's number — and the young man, dubbed by the faithful "Joe Mauer with more power," repaid the courtesy at once, driving the second pitch he saw some 380 feet to the center-field warning track. "It gave me straight chills," he said of the reception. The ball was run down — and here the pastime's sense of theater bears noting — by Tristan Peters, the White Stockings' rookie whose five-game home-run streak this paper has chronicled all week, and whose vigil upon the all-time mark of eight ended quietly the same evening: a single in four trips, no homer, the streak dead at five and the club record shared. Jenkins finished one-for-three with a walk and his first big-league hit, his manager Shelton pronouncing the whole evening "really impressive." One rookie's candle out, another's lit, and the Herald's lamp-trimmers stay busy.

THE PROTOCOL DESK: WEBB, A GENTLEMAN OF 204 GAMES' STANDING, IS EJECTED AT LAST — AND VITELLO MAKES IT TWICE IN THREE DAYS

The umpiring estate collected two notable scalps by the Bay on Friday. Logan Webb, who in 204 major-league games had never once been invited to leave one, was ejected from the San Francisco dugout for expressing — in what he conceded was an ungentlemanly tone — his opinion of two third-inning calls that undid the rookie Tidwell: an offering to Nootbaar called a ball where Webb saw strike three, and a fair-ball ruling in the same frame, the inning swelling to five Arizona runs behind Carroll's homer. "I don't think I get mad at umpires very often," Webb testified. "I thought that inning just didn't need to happen." His manager Vitello followed him to the showers directly — the rookie skipper's second ejection in three days and fifth of the season, a pace that would have done the old Baltimore Orioles proud. "I was hot before Tony was," Webb confessed, "and I think I got him hot." The Herald, which only Thursday related a missed balk gone unremedied in the desert nine's favor, observes that the umpiring estate and the National's West are developing a lively correspondence.

The Rest of the Card

GOLDSCHMIDT SUPPLIES THE RUN, SCHLITTLER THE TWO HUNDREDTH STRIKEOUT, AND BELLINGER THE THROW: YANKEES 1, FENWAY MEN 0

The guard this paper posted at the Bronx gate yesterday morning held it: Cam Schlittler, facing the club he rooted for as a boy, pitched scorelessly into the sixth — five walks survived, eight strikeouts collected, the two hundredth of his season among them, his earned-run figure now a league-best 2.09 — and Paul Goldschmidt's third-inning homer, his seventeenth, stood as the game's entire commerce. The Fenway men put five hits and six walks aboard and cashed none of them, Bellinger's seventh-inning throw from left arriving on one hop to the catcher Wells to cut down Rafaela and close an inning-ending double play, and Bednar sealed his one-and-thirtieth save. The season's series between the ancient rivals stands level at five apiece with three to play — a twin bill this very day, as the desk note relates — and New York's grip on the top wild-card chair measures three full games over Boston.

EIGHTY VICTORIES, A NEW BALLPARK, AND A CATCH THAT TOURED THE BULLPEN FURNITURE: TAMPA MEN 9, FRIARS 4

On the day the county blessed their Forever Home, the Tampa men became the first American League club to eighty victories, hanging five fourth-inning runs upon San Diego and never glancing back. Yandy Díaz homered his twentieth and drove in two, Mullins added his fourteenth over the fan-brushed right-field wall — reviewed and upheld — and Simpson stole two bases to reach seven-and-thirty, while McClanahan took the win. The defensive jewel belonged to DeLuca, who chased Fermin's foul pop at a dead sprint and slid clean into the home bullpen, fetching up against the bench with the ball secured — "as good of an outfield play as you're going to see," ruled his manager Cash. Merrill's two-run homer was the visitors' best answer; the Friars' hold on the National's last chair, as the card below relates, thinned to half a game by nightfall.

STOTT IS ROBBED OVER THE WALL, SO SOSA EMPTIES THE BASES INSTEAD: BROTHERLY LOVE NINE 5, HALOS 3

The ninth inning in Anaheim staged a full evening's theater in the span of five batters. The Halos led three-to-one — their runs banked in the first, two of them arriving by wild pitch — when Wade Meckler, fresh from the concussion list, leapt into the right-field stands to rob Stott of a three-run homer, a theft that ought to have decided matters. Two batters later the bases were full against the laboring Joyce, eleven strikes in six-and-twenty pitches, and the pinch-hitter Edmundo Sosa struck the relief man Peralta's offering to center for a grand slam placed beyond even Trout's compass — the first Philadelphia man to hit a go-ahead slam in the ninth with two out since Victorino in 2009, and the club's second stunning ninth-inning resurrection inside a week. Four runs batted in for Sosa, a second save for Bowlan's ledger by way of McFarlane's win, and the Brotherly Love nine hold their wild-card chair at three games' cushion.

ELEVEN OF TWELVE FOR THE KANSAS CITY MEN, AND CLEVELAND'S SEVEN-GAME PROCESSION HALTS AT THE WHITEWASH: ROYALS 3, LAKE ERIE MEN 0

The collision this paper appointed at yesterday's close went entirely to the visitors: Wacha and the relief corps blanked the Lake Erie men on six hits, Witt doubled and scored on Perez's fifth-inning groundout, and Carter Jensen — whose record-keeping leadoff homer graced Thursday's number — closed the accounts with a two-run blast in the ninth, his nineteenth. So dies Cleveland's seven-game winning streak, un-mourned by a Kansas City nine that has now won eleven of its last twelve; Bibee absorbed the loss, his fourteenth, and Cruz sealed his sixth save. The Central's arithmetic obliges the wild-card table instead: Cleveland's hold on the American's last chair is two games over Texas and Baltimore both, and the rubber of this set goes at 4:10 this afternoon, Lynch opposing Griffin and his gaudy fifteen-and-four.

A FOUR-RUN EIGHTH FALLS ONE SHORT, AND FRIEDL — THE WAIVED MAN — SUPPLIES THE CUSHION: QUEEN CITY NINE 10, CUBS 8

A slugging carnival at Wrigley ran to six-and-twenty hits, and the Queen City nine banked just enough of them. Trailing three-to-two after Sal Stewart's nine-and-twentieth homer had chipped at Chicago's early lead, they hung five upon the sixth inning — Trevino's equalizer, Stewart's run-scoring single, and Stephenson's three-run blast the heavy freight — and Stewart's two runs batted in swell the National's leading ledger to one hundred and two. The Cubs answered with four in the eighth behind Ramírez's three-run homer and Suzuki's third hit, drawing to nine-and-eight, whereupon TJ Friedl — set upon the waiver wire Wednesday beside Suárez, whose slam that same night these pages sang — homered in the ninth for the margin that held. Lowder took the win, Pagán his eighteenth save, and the North Side nine have now dropped three running, their wild-card cushion at four games.

FIVE STRAIGHT FOR THE BRAVES, AND ACUÑA ANSWERS HIS DAY OFF WITH THREE HITS: ATLANTA 6, MILE HIGH NINE 4

Sat down Thursday by his manager Weiss for a breather, Ronald Acuña Jr. returned Friday with his first three-hit evening of the season, a fifth-inning double leaving his bat at 108 miles to the hour just ahead of Michael Harris II's two-run homer — the center fielder's two-and-twentieth, part of a three-hit, three-runs-batted-in night of his own. The Mile High nine closed within a single run by the fifth — McCarthy's sacrifice fly, Goodman's run-scoring single, and Rumfield's groundout doing the work — and within two on Castro's seventh-inning sacrifice fly, but Iglesias sealed his nine-and-twentieth save behind the winner Holmes, and the Braves' streak runs to five — their lead in the National's East a comfortable five games over Philadelphia, and the pursuit of Los Angeles for the second first-round bye now a matter of a single game.

CEASE MAKES HIS CASE IN SIX TIDY INNINGS, AND OKAMOTO DRIVES HOME THREE: JAYS 8, MARINERS 1

An evening after boos chased them from their own yard, the Jays handed the ball to Dylan Cease and were rewarded with the customary: six innings, one run, eight strikeouts — his league-leading total now two hundred seventeen — in an eight-to-one settling of Seattle. The wires already frame the American's Cy Young argument as Cease against Schlittler, and Friday's twin gems, pitched hours apart, will not simplify the jury's work. Okamoto drove home three with his seven-and-twentieth homer among them, Springer and Lukes added blasts of their own, and Canzone's leadoff homer for the visitors was Seattle's whole account. The Jays thus stand two games and a half from Cleveland's wild-card chair; the Mariners, four astern of Houston's division crown, drift.

HENDERSON GOES SEVEN AGAIN, CONTRERAS DRIVES HOME THREE, AND THE BEST RECORD FATTENS: BREW CREW 6, LONE STAR NINE 1

Logan Henderson, Milwaukee's Mr. Reliable by his own clubhouse's coinage, matched his career high with seven innings in a six-to-one dispatch of Texas, running his ledger to nine-and-two while William Contreras drove in three and the fourteen-hit attack ground along behind him. Two Texas hits the whole evening — Jansen's homer the lone run — and the Brew Crew stand at four-and-eighty victories against one-and-fifty defeats, the game's best record, three-and-thirty games above the break-even line and eight clear of the Cubs in the Central. Their manager Murphy, offered every milestone in the ledger, wanted none of it: "This is a really young team. You can't divide their attention." The Lone Star nine, for their part, slip two games from the American's wild-card row.

FOUR IN THE FIRST HOLD UP AT TARGET FIELD, AND THE PALE HOSE PASS A MILESTONE NO RESURRECTED CLUB HAD REACHED: PALE HOSE 7, TWIN CITIES NINE 4

Colson Montgomery's three-run homer, his eight-and-twentieth, capped a four-run first from which Minnesota never quite recovered, though Lee's two-run blast and Clemens's solo answered by the second. Benintendi doubled home the fifth run, two more crossed by passed ball and wild pitch, and Taylor took the decision ahead of Hudson's sixth save. The one-and-seventieth victory carries its own freight: no club that had suffered three consecutive seasons of a hundred losses had ever before won more than seventy games in the year following, and the South Siders passed the 2014 Houstons, the 1965 Senators, and the 1925 Boston Braves in a single evening. Their grip on the Central stands at three games and a half over Cleveland; the debutant Jenkins's evening, and Peters's ended vigil, are the debut desk's business above.

BROWN STRIKES OUT TEN IN QUEENS, AND THE WEST'S CROWN GAINS ANOTHER GAME'S PURCHASE: HOUSTON NINE 3, METS 1

Winless through four August starts, Hunter Brown chose Citi Field to remember himself: ten strikeouts across six innings and two-thirds, one run allowed, and the first Houston starter to complete six innings since the tenth of August — a drought of fourteen games between quality starts that had worn the bullpen to the nub. Varsho singled home two in the three-run sixth and Diaz cashed the third; Hader closed his twentieth save. "That's the Hunter that we're used to seeing," pronounced the manager Espada. The Houston nine have taken three of four on their New York excursion, and the West's crown — half a game wide when this week opened — now measures two full games over Texas, the tiebreaker in Houston's pocket besides.

TEN INNINGS BY THE BAY OF SACRAMENTO, A RUNNER CUT DOWN AT THE DOOR, AND THE O'S TAKE IT: ORIOLES 4, MACKMEN 3

A two-nought Baltimore lead built in the second held until the Mackmen chipped it away — Heim's homer in the seventh, and in the eighth Butler's single cashing Bolte while Beavers, from left field, threw McNeil out at the plate to keep the account level. The tenth settled it: Mayo and Encarnacion-Strand singled home a run apiece, Gelof's answering single retrieved one, and Hoppe recorded the final outs for his first save behind the winner Kittredge. The O's thus open their western swing a game to the good, two games from Cleveland's wild-card chair; the Athletics, spoilers of cheerful reputation, will resume the argument at 10:05 this evening.

THREE PITTSBURGH ERRORS, ONE CROOKS HOMER, AND THE CARDS COLLECT QUIETLY: REDBIRDS 4, CORSAIRS 1

The young catcher Crooks supplied the decisive blow, a two-run homer in the third — his fifth — and St. Louis added single runs on Church's sacrifice fly and a Pittsburgh throwing error, which was fitting bookkeeping on an evening the Corsairs kicked the ball thrice. Mathews took his first victory of the season, Stanek sealed his second save, and Triolo's run-scoring single stood as the visitors' entire offense. Two straight now for the Redbirds, who sit four games and a half from the National's last chair — arithmetic that obliges them to keep winning and the four clubs above them to oblige by losing.

A FIVE-RUN THIRD AND A TEN-RUN EVENING IN THE DESERT'S FAVOR: DESERT NINE 10, JINTS 6

The ejections are the protocol desk's business above; the baseball was emphatic enough on its own. Nootbaar opened the game with a leadoff homer, Carroll struck a two-run blast in the five-run third — his nineteenth, part of three driven in — and Tawa followed directly with a three-run shot of his own as the Desert nine buried San Francisco ten-to-six. Eldridge homered and doubled, and Koss added a two-run blast for the home nine's dignity; Carrillo took the win over the rookie Tidwell. The prize is the arithmetic: with San Diego beaten at Tampa Bay, Arizona stands but half a game from the National's final chair — and the two clubs meet again twice this very day, a twin bill at 4:05 and 10:05 by the Eastern clock, with the whole of the chase compressed into one Saturday by the Bay.

FIVE IN THE THIRD, FOUR IN THE SEVENTH, AND TWO RUNS DELIVERED BY A SINGLE WILD PITCH: SENATORS 9, GULF STREAM NINE 2

The Senators did their week's scoring in two installments. The third inning produced five — two of its runs crossing upon a single wild pitch, a delivery that will trouble somebody's sleep, before Brady House cleared the bases' remainder with a three-run homer, his tenth — and the seventh added four more, Ford's homer, Crews's two-run double, and Lile's triple among the freight. Kent took the decision; Heriberto Hernández's one-and-twentieth homer and Edwards's run-scoring single were the whole of the Gulf Stream nine's reply. Two straight now for Washington, and the clubs return to it at 12:15 on the morrow — the Fish, whose wild-card deficit stands at four games, in some hurry to stop the bleeding.

The morning tables, briefly surveyed. In the American: Tampa Bay, first of that league to eighty victories, holds the East by four over New York with Boston seven astern; the Pale Hose keep the Central by three and a half over a Cleveland nine whose streak died at seven; Houston's crown in the West is two games wide over Texas; and the wild-card row reads New York, Boston, and Cleveland's last chair by two over Texas and Baltimore, with Toronto two and a half back. In the National: Atlanta by five in the East, Milwaukee by eight in the Central, Los Angeles by nine in the West, and the chairs behind them — Chicago's cushion four, Philadelphia's three, and San Diego's final seat now half a game ahead of the desert, with Miami four back and St. Louis four and a half. Today's card runs to seventeen engagements upon fifteen grounds, all verified against the schedule, and the desk directs the reader's eye to three appointments: in the Bronx, the ancient rivals play a twin bill at 1:05 and 7:15, the season series level at five apiece and Fried, restored from his elbow's complaint, appointed to the evening half; by the other Bay, the Desert nine and the Jints likewise go twice, at 4:05 and 10:05, with San Diego's half-game chair the stakes and the Friars engaged at Tampa Bay at 4:10; and at 4:10 in Cleveland the Royals' eleven-of-twelve surge meets Griffin and his fifteen-and-four in the rubber of the set. The champions and the Tigers resume at 1:10, and Sunday at 1:40 may yet bring the unicorn to the mound, as the ward above relates.
