entry.title: THE DESK'S APPOINTMENT IS KEPT, THOUGH NOT AS PHILADELPHIA DREW IT: RALEIGH, LONG BECALMED, STRIKES THREE HOME RUNS, WHEELER IS CHASED, AND THE STREAK DIES AT NINE — MARINERS 9, PHILADELPHIAS 2
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 48 · Tuesday, the Five-and-Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 10 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

THE DESK'S APPOINTMENT IS KEPT, THOUGH NOT AS PHILADELPHIA DREW IT: RALEIGH, LONG BECALMED, STRIKES THREE HOME RUNS, WHEELER IS CHASED, AND THE STREAK DIES AT NINE — MARINERS 9, PHILADELPHIAS 2

The catcher who began the evening batting .159 ends it the thirteenth man in Seattle's annals with a three-homer game — a two-run blast to crown a five-run first, a back-to-back salvo with Young to open the fifth, a solo shot in the seventh — while the Philadelphia nine, riders of a season-best winning streak this paper has chronicled at every length, are sent to bed with two runs and a battered ace

The reader will recall that yesterday's desk note directed all eyes to Seattle at 9:40 Eastern, where Wheeler and his ten victories were to oppose Gilbert, and the Philadelphia nine were to unpack a nine-game winning streak from their westward luggage. The appointment was kept to the minute; the script was burned in the first inning. Philadelphia scratched a run from Bohm's ground-out, whereupon the home nine answered with five — Julio Rodríguez clearing the fence with two aboard for his twentieth, and Cal Raleigh, the switch-hitting catcher whose season has been one long penance at .159, capping the frame with a two-run blast. It was the first sentence of the finest chapter of his life.

For Raleigh opened the fifth with another homer, Cole Young followed him over the wall on the very next argument — the back-to-back salvo that chased Wheeler from the premises — and in the seventh he struck a third, a solo shot off the reliever Shugart, all three driven to the right-field quarter. No man had ever seen him do it: "I had never done that before — at any level. So, hard to fathom, and it was a fun night," the author testified, having gone three-for-three with a walk and lifted his average from .159 to .167. The researchers certify him the thirteenth Mariner to strike three home runs in a game — the last being his clubmate Canzone only last September — and the only other Seattle catcher ever to do it is one Dan Wilson, who now writes the lineup card on which Raleigh's name appears. The manager's fraternity, one supposes, has its own ways of passing down a trade secret.

The wreckage on the other side was considerable: Wheeler, sovereign of ten victories against four defeats at the evening's start, was relieved of nine hits, eight runs, and four home runs inside four innings, and departs at ten-and-five; Realmuto's ninth homer was the visitors' lone late ornament. Logan Gilbert took the decision, his eleventh, on five workmanlike innings. Thus the finest streak of Philadelphia's season perishes at nine — the Philadelphias remain three and a half astern of Atlanta and keep the National's second wild-card chair, so the mourning need not be prolonged — while the Emerald City nine, who gave their faithful two walk-off deliverances Friday and Saturday and then absorbed Chicago's nineteen-run sermon Sunday, have now taken three of four in that yard and stand three games from the American's final chair. The Sound, it appears, declines to be dull.

News Around the League

THE FRONT-OFFICE DESK: HOUSTON AND ITS GENERAL MANAGER PART COMPANY IN THE THICK OF A PENNANT RACE, AND ESPADA RETURNS TO HIS POST

The Houston club and its general manager Dana Brown have parted ways, the club announcing Monday what the wires describe as a mutual conclusion to a tenure begun in January of 2023 — two division titles to its credit, a contract expiring with the season, and a club that has lost six of its last eight engagements. The portfolio passes in commission to the assistant general managers Cook, Dickey, and Huff and to the senior adviser Jeff Bagwell, with the owner Crane overseeing the baseball operations himself through the transition — an arrangement the Herald observes without endorsement, owners' oversight of baseball matters having a mixed record in the annals. The timing is remarkable: the Houstons wake this morning half a game astern of the Lone Star nine in the West, their crown mislaid in idleness. There is gentler news from the same clubhouse — the manager Joe Espada, called away by a family emergency, rejoins his men for this evening's opener in the Bronx, which the schedule confirms for five minutes past seven, Eastern.

THE LABOR QUESTION: MANFRED PLEDGES THAT BASEBALL MEANS TO PLAY IN '27, AND THE HERALD TAKES THE PLEDGE UNDER ADVISEMENT

From the same Williamsport broadcast that appointed next year's Little League Classic — as this paper related Monday — the Commissioner Manfred addressed the graver matter: the collective bargain between the clubs and the players' union expires at one minute before midnight on the first of December, and the question of the 2027 season hangs upon its renewal. "We want to make a deal. We want to play baseball next year. We're planning on playing baseball next year," the Commissioner declared, reporting weekly conferences between the parties. The Herald prints the pledge faithfully and notes what follows it: the owners' chief object in the negotiation is a salary cap, the union's answer that the economic order wants no such overhaul — their asks running instead to a raised minimum wage, a loosened luxury-tax collar, and a fattened bonus pool for the young and underpaid — and the wires' sober assessment that, failing a bargain by the deadline, the likeliest course is a lockout of the players by the owners, shutting the game's business entire. On the merits the Herald's sympathies are of record and lie with the workingmen; as for the owners' capacity to pay, the reader need only consult the counting-house item below, where a franchise has just changed hands for a sum with a b in it.

THE COUNTING-HOUSE DESK: SAN DIEGO'S NEW PROPRIETORS ARRIVE WITH A SONG, TWO JERSEYS, AND THREE THOUSAND NINE HUNDRED MILLIONS

The Padres formally presented their new proprietors Monday at Petco Park: Jose E. Feliciano and Kwanza Jones, husband and wife, who purchased the franchise at a valuation of $3.9 billion — the grandest price ever fetched by a baseball club — and were approved without dissent by the other nine-and-twenty owners a week past. The hour-long introduction opened with a song of Ms. Jones' own composition and closed with the couple in customized jerseys, and between came the substance: the purchase styled a "family investment," a pledge to spend "ambitiously" yet "judiciously," and repeated homage to the late Peter Seidler, whose open-handed stewardship the faithful of San Diego remember warmly. "We wanna win," Mr. Feliciano summarized. The Herald extends its welcome, notes that forty thousand four hundred forty-seven attended that very evening's twelve-inning engagement — the card below has its sorrows — and files the sale price where it belongs: in the ledger consulted whenever an owner next pleads poverty.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: FAIRBANKS' ARM SOUNDS ITS ALARM AGAIN, TOGLIA AND EMERSON GO UNDER THE KNIFE, AND PHOENIX HOPES FOR MARTE WITHIN THE WEEK

The gravest entry issues from Miami, where the closer Pete Fairbanks — seven seasons a Ray, now the Marlins' keeper of eighteen saves — felt nerve irritation and numbness through his throwing arm in the ninth inning Monday, walked the only man he faced, and departed; the walk became the deciding run, as the card below relates. The complaint is an old acquaintance, having cost him three weeks after a like episode in April — "Both of them weren't good," the patient allowed — and he submits to examinations this day.

Two seasons end upon the operating table. In Cincinnati, Michael Toglia — whose wounded shoulder this paper's ward first recorded Saturday — has his torn labrum repaired Tuesday, the price of a diving catch made in Arizona; the manager Francona reports the man had sworn he could play, which is admirable and immaterial. And in Seattle, the rookie shortstop Colt Emerson, one-and-twenty years of age and owner of an eight-year fortune signed before he had played a major-league game, will have a wrist tendon set right Wednesday, his trying freshman season closed at .190; the club expects him whole by spring, and his clubmate Bryan Woo, pronounced fit, takes his scheduled turn Wednesday. In Phoenix, at last, a hopeful line: the Diamondbacks believe Ketel Marte — whose saga this paper has chronicled past all appetite — may rejoin the lineup within the week.

THE MILESTONE DESK: STEWART STANDS TWO SHORT OF A HUNDRED, THE CARDINAL PAIR LURK AT SIX-AND-NINETY, AND ALVAREZ'S CROWN OF THREE SURVIVES AN IDLE MONDAY

The freshman Sal Stewart of Cincinnati was held without a tally in Monday's whitewash by the Bay, and so stands where he stood: eight-and-ninety runs driven home, master of all baseball's table, two short of the hundred mark and still pursuing the distinction — unclaimed by any rookie since 1950 — of leading the major leagues outright. His shadow has two heads and wears Cardinal red: Burleson and Walker, six-and-ninety apiece, idle Monday and losing no ground. In the American the arithmetic likewise kept the Sabbath: Yordan Alvarez, his club unengaged, holds his crown of three untouched — .320, six-and-thirty homers, ninety runs driven in, first in every column — though the Herald notes Caminero of Tampa Bay one homer astern, and observes that a Triple Crown defended from a deck chair is defended all the same.

The Rest of the Card

TWO IN THE NINTH, TAKEN FROM A WOUNDED HAND: RED SOX 4, MIAMI NINE 2, AND THE COUNT RUNS TO FOUR STRAIGHT

For eight innings Miami had the better of the argument's texture — Alcantara dealing seven innings of one-run ball — and none of its arithmetic: Abreu scored the equalizer on a wild pitch in the eighth, and in the ninth the stricken Fairbanks walked Gasper and departed with the arm trouble the infirmary ward records, whereupon Seigler tripled home the go-ahead run and Sogard singled in another. Chapman barred the door for his thirtieth save. Four straight now for the New Englanders, seven of ten, their wild-card cushion ample; the walk Fairbanks issued became his defeat, and the Miami nine slip to four astern of the National's final chair.

THE MACHINE DOES NOT REQUIRE DRAMA: GULF COAST CLUB 4, TIGERS 1, AND RASMUSSEN MAKES IT SEVEN RUNNING

Drew Rasmussen collected his seventh consecutive victory by the simplest of recipes — six innings, three hits, one run — while Aranda supplied a sixteenth homer and two runs driven in, Simpson dropped a bunt for a run with the insolence of a man batting .312, and Baker sealed his eight-and-thirtieth save. The league leaders thus hold their three-and-a-half-game advantage over the Bronx; the Tigers, whose evening amounted to five hits and Callahan's sacrifice fly, have now dropped six running — one victory in their last ten — and the Motor City's September reading grows grim.

THE SHORTSTOP RETURNS AND THE OFFENSE REMEMBERS ITSELF: POTOMAC NINE 13, MILE HIGH NINE 3

Restored to the lineup, CJ Abrams scored twice, stole twice, and presided over a thirteen-run festival — Daylen Lile the chief celebrant with three hits, a sixteenth homer, and five runs driven in, Vivas adding three hits of his own — while Cade Cavalli struck out seven across six innings for his twelfth victory. "Now we go," runs the clubhouse verdict on the wires. For Colorado, Tovar's two hits and a homer were the ornament on a seventh consecutive defeat; the Mile High nine departed the Capital outscored beyond argument.

SEAGER CONDUCTS, BURGER AND LANGFORD SUPPLY THE BRASS, AND THE WEST'S CROWN FINDS A SINGLE HEAD: LONE STAR NINE 11, CHICAGOS 2

Texas struck early, often, and then again: Seager three hits and three runs driven in with a pair of doubles, Burger a two-and-twentieth homer among his two hits, Langford a fifteenth to close the accounts, fourteen hits in the whole demonstration behind Rocker's eight strikeouts. The visiting defense contributed its own theater — Nimmo at full extension above the right-field fence to rob Benintendi outright — and the home dugout its melancholy: Pederson, denied upon a challenge to the automated ball-strike arbiter, banged his bat and was invited to leave. Peters' two-run homer, the tenth of his year, was all the Chicagos could answer; and with Houston idle, the Lone Star nine take sole possession of the West's chair at six-and-sixty wins against the like number of defeats — a crown at the break-even line, but a crown unshared.

A HOMER FOR THE VISITING PEWS: GUARDIANS 4, SERAPHS 2, AND THE STREAK REACHES FIVE

Austin Hedges, with his parents in attendance, struck a two-run homer — his fifth — that stood as the difference, Kwan collected two hits, and Messick pitched to his tenth victory before Smith closed his four-and-thirtieth save. A fifth consecutive victory for Cleveland, seven of ten by the ledger, and the consequence is recorded in this evening's desk note: the American's final wild-card chair, so long a boarding-house, now holds a single tenant. The Seraphs' consolations were two hits off the bench from Lowe and the certainty of a warm evening in Anaheim.

GAUSMAN DEALS SEVEN SPOTLESS AND THE DESERT GOES HUNGRY: CUBS 7, DIAMONDBACKS 0

Kevin Gausman threw seven scoreless innings on three hits, and his employers, fresh from Sunday's nineteen-run sermon by the Sound, kept the pulpit: Conforto three hits with a twelfth homer, Carson Kelly an eighth, the rookie Pedro Ramírez a triple among his two hits, and a three-run sixth followed by two more in the seventh to end the suspense. The whitewash is Chicago's second consecutive victory; for Arizona it is a graver matter, the Diamondbacks falling two games astern of San Diego in the pursuit of the National's final chair — with, as the infirmary ward relates, hope of Marte's return the week's best medicine.

BUXTON SCORES FROM EVERYWHERE AND THE NINTH-INNING RALLY ARRIVES TOO LATE: NORTH STARS 9, WHITE ELEPHANTS 6

Buxton crossed the plate four times upon three hits, the rookie Culpepper collected four hits, Bell drove home three, and Zebby Matthews carried a commanding evening through seven innings; when the White Elephants awoke for four runs in the ninth — McNeil, Gelof, and Butler doubling in file — the awakening was academic, and Morris recorded the final out for the save. Sixteen hits for the North Stars, who remain two from the American's final chair; for the Athletics, a twelve-hit evening wasted, and a reminder that arithmetic performed in the ninth earns no interest.

TWELVE INNINGS, FOUR HOURS AND TEN MINUTES, AND ONE RUN TO SHOW THE NEW PROPRIETORS: CORSAIRS 3, PADRES 2

On the very evening San Diego's new owners took their bows — the counting-house desk has the ceremony — forty thousand four hundred forty-seven watched the home nine spend twelve innings discovering that the visitors would not oblige. Valdez's fifteenth homer and Flores Jr.'s double built Pittsburgh's lead; a balk and Cronenworth's eighth-inning single leveled it; and in the twelfth Nick Gonzales — he of the .308 average, second in the National's batting table — singled home Triolo for the verdict. Yates profited, Ramírez sealed his second save, and the Padres' grip on the National's third chair holds at two games over Arizona, the evening's four hours and ten minutes notwithstanding.

FIVE RUNS IN TWO INNINGS OFF THE FOURTEEN-GAME WINNER, AND THE SHORN GIANTS SHUT OUT THE REDS: JINTS 5, CINCINNATI 0

The San Franciscans took the field Monday having consigned four men to the infirmary in a single day's transactions — Adames' elbow, Bericoto's knee, Brubaker's ribs, and Eldridge away on bereavement — recalled five from Sacramento to fill the pews, and then played their finest game in a fortnight: five runs inside two innings off Chase Burns, owner of fourteen victories against but two defeats at the evening's start, crowned by Devers' three-run homer, his seven-and-twentieth. Six pitchers passed the whitewash hand to hand, Foley taking the decision. Burns falls to fourteen-and-three; the Reds, blanked on five hits and further bereaved of Toglia — see the ward — find their September arithmetic unimproved.

The arithmetic desk reports a morning of consequence at both ends of the American's ledger. The final wild-card chair, which has been let by the room and by the half-week all month, this morning holds one tenant alone: Cleveland, winners of five running, at six-and-sixty wins against six-and-sixty defeats — and thus, for the first time in this desk's recent chronicle, the chair's occupant sits no lower than the break-even line. The eviction was accomplished upward, Texas departing the wild-card row entirely to take sole possession of the West's crown at the identical break-even figure, with Houston half a game astern in both accountings and this morning without a general manager besides, as the front-office desk relates. Behind Cleveland: Houston at half a game, Minnesota and Toronto two, Baltimore two and a half, Seattle three. In the National the chairs hold — the Cubs, Philadelphia with its streak freshly buried at nine, and San Diego, with Arizona two astern and Miami four. The card this evening runs to the full fifteen engagements, all verified against the schedule: the Brewers send Harrison and his ten victories to Flushing at 7:10; the champions and the Atlantas resume their collision at 7:15, Glasnow opposing Elder; Espada resumes his post as the Houstons open in the Bronx at 7:05; and by the Pacific, Skenes and his hundred-and-seventy-one strikeouts visit San Diego at 9:40. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: TWO OUT IN THE NINTH, FOUR RUNS IN ARREARS — AND SIX STILL TO COME: SCHWARBER'S NINE-AND-THIRTIETH SETTLES IT, PHILLIES 6, CARDINALS 4, AND THE STREAK IS NINE
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 47 · Monday, the Four-and-Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

TWO OUT IN THE NINTH, FOUR RUNS IN ARREARS — AND SIX STILL TO COME: SCHWARBER'S NINE-AND-THIRTIETH SETTLES IT, PHILLIES 6, CARDINALS 4, AND THE STREAK IS NINE

Down to their final out at Citizens Bank Park, the Philadelphians load the bases against O'Brien, sovereign of the National's saves table, whereupon Sosa's two-strike double clears them, De La Cruz knots the score, and Schwarber — in his own words reduced to shocked disbelief — launches the two-run blast that makes the winning streak nine and the walk-off the second of the series

Through eight innings Sunday evening at Citizens Bank Park the game belonged wholly to St. Louis, and the ledger said so without ornament: four runs to none, the tallies gathered patiently — Burleson driving home a run apiece in the first and the fourth, Fermín lifting his sixth homer over the left-center barrier in the fifth, Wetherholt cashing another in the seventh. To guard the treasure the Redbirds summoned O'Brien, keeper of three-and-thirty saves and the National League's leader in that commerce, and when he had secured two outs the arithmetic gave Philadelphia scarcely a prayer.

What followed will be retold in that city for some seasons. The bases filled. Edmundo Sosa, down to his final strike, doubled to clear them — Harper, Realmuto, and Crawford racing home in single file — and the deficit shrank to one. Bryan De La Cruz singled, the inning's fourth two-strike hit, and the game stood level at four. Then Kyle Schwarber, whose nine-and-thirty home runs already led the National League, sent the next argument soaring into the Philadelphia night and stood a moment at the plate in what he later called "shocked disbelief," equal to nothing but a tossed helmet, a flung bat, and a slow lap into the arms of the assembled. Six runs in the ninth, all with two out; a 6-4 verdict; a winning streak now nine games long. "We're the Phillies; I can't say I'm really surprised," offered Sosa afterward, and the standings second the motion: nine victories in their last ten leave the Brotherly Love nine three games astern of Atlanta in the East and firmly seated in the wild-card row. It is, the record shows, the second time in three evenings St. Louis has been beaten in Philadelphia at the game's final turn — Friday by Bohm's triple in the tenth, as this paper related Saturday — and the poor Redbirds must now depart while the victors fly west, where a nine-game expedition through Seattle, Anaheim, and Phoenix opens this very night.

News Around the League

THE UNICORN PAWS AT THE GATE: OHTANI THROWS THIRTY PITCHES AT LIVING BATSMEN, AND THE CLUB APPOINTS HIS RETURN FOR THE NEXT HOMESTAND

Seven weeks removed from his last turn upon the mound, Shohei Ohtani faced live hitters at Chavez Ravine before Saturday's engagement — thirty pitches across six simulated plate appearances, his opposite number the convalescing catcher Will Smith — and the Los Angeles management now declares him likely to start during the club's next homestand. The great man last pitched July the third, having compiled eight victories against two defeats and an earned-run figure of 1.79 across fourteen starts before a balky left knee intervened. "If it were up to Shohei," testified the manager Roberts, "he'd be in a game in a few days." The Herald notes that the Angelenos, winners of six running, have scarcely missed a beat in his mound absence — a fact that ought to terrify the rest of the National League rather than comfort it.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: WEATHERS JOINS THE YANKEE SICK-LIST, JUDGE TAKES UP THE TEE, ANTHONY'S RETURN IS APPOINTED, AND PHOENIX LOSES SOROKA

The Yankee infirmary, already crowded, admits another: Ryan Weathers went to the fifteen-day list Sunday with a low-grade flexor strain of the left forearm, though the club professes optimism he pitches again this season. Elsewhere in that ward, Judge has taken to striking a ball from a tee — modest commerce, but commerce — while Fried threw a bullpen of six-and-twenty pitches Saturday and may return when first eligible; Stanton, both calves now in conspiracy against him, may be finished for the year, as this paper reported yesterday.

In Boston the news runs brighter: the rookie Roman Anthony transfers his rehabilitation to Worcester on Tuesday and could rejoin the Boston club during their engagement in New York at the week's end. In Phoenix, darker: the Diamondbacks, whose trying week began with the Marte affair this paper has chronicled, dispatched Michael Soroka to the fifteen-day list with inflammation of the right shoulder, a day after he labored for his command. And in the champions' camp, Glasnow is appointed to come off the list and start Tuesday at Atlanta — where, the schedule confirms, the Dodgers and Braves open their engagement tomorrow evening.

THE MONUMENT DESK: EIGHT HUNDRED POUNDS OF BRONZE FOR THE MAN FROM MAPLE RIDGE, AND TEARS AT TWENTIETH AND BLAKE

Sunday morning outside Coors Field, to the unlikely accompaniment of "Crazy Train," a purple shroud came away and Larry Walker beheld himself fifteen feet tall and eight hundred pounds of bronze, bat hoisted to the sky — the first Hall of Famer of the Colorado franchise, now standing sentry at the main gate at Twentieth and Blake. The man from Maple Ridge, British Columbia, nine-and-fifty years of age, carried his speech gracefully until he reached his father, Larry the elder, seated near at hand, whereupon the tears arrived. In attendance: Ferguson Jenkins, the only other Canadian enshrined at Cooperstown; Todd Helton, the Rockies' other Hall man; and Bob Gebhard, the original general manager who brought Walker to Colorado. The honoree's own verdict on his likeness: "Guess that's a way to slow me down."

THE ALMANAC DESK: WILLIAMSPORT ENGAGES THE JAYS AND THE CUBS FOR THE TENTH CLASSIC, ANNO 2027

The ink was scarcely dry on the ninth Little League Classic — of which more below, the Braves having taken it — when the Commissioner Manfred, joining Sunday night's broadcast from Williamsport, announced the tenth: the Toronto Blue Jays and the Chicago Cubs shall meet at that shrine on Thursday, the nineteenth of August, 2027. The fixture, hosted as ever in connection with the Little League World Series, will mark the annual showcase's tenth year, and Major Leaguers from both nines will spend the day among the twelve-year-olds before the evening's business. The Herald, which watched this year's edition work its particular magic upon grown professionals, pronounces the institution in rude health.

THE MILESTONE DESK: STEWART AT EIGHT-AND-NINETY, TWO CARDINALS LEVEL AT SIX-AND-NINETY, AND THE CROWN OF THREE ENDURES

The freshman Sal Stewart of Cincinnati, undeterred by his club's Sunday defeat in the desert, drove home another run and stands now at eight-and-ninety on the season — still the master of all baseball's runs-batted-in table, still chasing the distinction, unclaimed by any rookie since 1950, of leading the major leagues outright. His pursuers have consolidated: Burleson's pair in the Philadelphia calamity draws him level with his clubmate Walker at six-and-ninety apiece, two St. Louis men sharing second place two tallies astern. In the American, meanwhile, Yordan Alvarez holds his crown of three yet again — a .320 average, six-and-thirty homers, ninety runs driven in, first in all three columns — even as his Houston nine contrive new ways to squander a Sunday, as the card below relates.

The Rest of the Card

THE WOUND IS STANCHED AS ADVERTISED: TAMPA MEN 3, BIRDS 1, WITH MARTINEZ'S THIRTEENTH AND BAKER'S SEVEN-AND-THIRTIETH

The matchup this paper flagged yesterday — Martinez against Baz, a three-game skid to be arrested — resolved precisely as Tampa Bay drew it up: a three-run sixth off singles from Caminero and Simpson, and Baker closing for his seven-and-thirtieth save, most in the American. Martinez's thirteenth victory keeps the Rays three games clear of the Bronx at the head of the East. Baltimore managed two hits all afternoon, both by Cowser, whose ninth-inning homer spared the Birds a whitewash; Baz, game but unlucky, falls to four-and-fourteen.

TWO, THEN THREE, THEN TWO MORE, AND THE PURSUIT IS MAINTAINED: HIGHLANDERS 8, MAPLE LEAF NINE 3

New York kept pace with the leaders by installments — two runs in the second, three in the sixth, two in the seventh, and Grisham's eighteenth homer for punctuation in the eighth — while eleven hits fell about the Toronto defense. Blackburn took the decision to five-and-two; Soriano bore the loss. Kirk's run-scoring single was the visitors' consolation, and the Highlanders remain three astern of Tampa Bay with a homestand against Houston beginning tomorrow.

A MAN MAY CLIMB A WALL AND STILL LOSE THE DAY: GULF STREAM NINE 6, WASHINGTONS 2

The Capital club's center fielder Jacob Young performed the afternoon's great larceny at loanDepot park, scaling the left-center barrier in two distinct climbs — in the manner of a human fly — to rob Heriberto Hernández of a drive struck at a hundred and five miles to the hour, and turning the theft into a double play besides. It availed Washington nothing: Miami fed steadily all evening, Mack and Crews doubling in runs, and the Marlins — one-and-forty victories now against but five-and-twenty defeats in their own yard — sent the Washingtons home from a road expedition concluded at one victory against eight defeats.

SIX RUNS DOWN, THEN SIX IN A SINGLE FRAME: MACKMEN 7, HOUSTON NINE 6, AND THE WEST'S CROWN SITS ON TWO UNEASY HEADS

Houston built a fortress by the fourth — Altuve's fourteenth homer, Paredes' seventeenth, six runs to none — and the Athletics burned it down in the fifth: Serven's three-run blast, Butler's double, Tommy White's two-run single, six tallies in the frame. Max Muncy's seventh homer in the seventh supplied the difference, and the Mackmen, last in the West, had beaten its leaders two days running. The consequence at the summit is remarkable: Houston and Texas now share the division's chair at five-and-sixty wins against six-and-sixty defeats — a crown worn jointly, and below the break-even line at that.

SALVY STEALS A BASE, THE CROWD STEALS A LOOK AT THE CALENDAR, AND THE STREAK REACHES EIGHT: ROYALS 11, MOTOR CITY NINE 7

The morning's baserunning conference at Kauffman Stadium was conducted, by all accounts uproariously, by Salvador Perez himself — and in the second inning the six-and-thirty-year-old backstop made good on his own sermon, swiping second base for the first time since July of 2021 and the first time in his home yard since 2017. "That feels even better than a home run," he testified. Thus inspirited, Kansas City piled five runs in the second behind Loftin's three-run homer and four more in the fifth, Rave clearing the fence, and survived Detroit's four-run reply — McGonigle's fourteenth among it — for an eighth consecutive victory, nine of their last ten. The Detroits have dropped five running.

PETERS AGAIN SUPPLIES THE LAST WORD: PALE HOSE 2, FLUSHING NINE 1, AND SENGA'S LUCKLESS LEDGER READS NOUGHT-AND-NINE

For the second time in three evenings the South Side settled its business at the final swing: Benintendi's double gave Chicago the lead in the eighth, Jared Young's single restored the level in the ninth, and Tristan Peters promptly unrestored it with his ninth homer, a walk-off blast to center. The cruelest line in the box belongs to Senga, who pitched well enough to win most evenings and fell instead to nought-and-nine on the season — a record that ought to be tried before a fairer court.

SIX SPOTLESS INNINGS FROM QUANTRILL, AND THE HOMESTAND CLOSES IN CREDIT: ARLINGTON MEN 5, HALOS 3

Cal Quantrill dealt six scoreless innings on six hits and six strikeouts, Texas banked three runs in the second and two in the fifth, and Latz weathered Neto's twenty-second homer in the late going for his six-and-twentieth save. Kikuchi absorbed the defeat. The Arlington men thus conclude their homestand a game to the good and share the West's summit with Houston — see above for the full accounting of that curious diarchy.

A SWEEP AT ALTITUDE, A FIFTEENTH VICTORY, AND A BEE WITH NO RESPECT FOR THE PROCEEDINGS: LAKE ERIE MEN 7, COLORADANS 2

Cleveland struck five runs inside two innings, Griffin ran his astonishing ledger to fifteen victories against four defeats, and the Guardians completed the sweep for a fourth consecutive win — cementing their joint tenancy of the American's last wild-card chair, of which the desk below has more. The afternoon's strangest wound was inflicted in the sixth, when the Colorado reliever Herget was stung upon the pitching arm by a bee in the very act of his duties ("I'm not a bee expert or whatever," he confessed). The Coloradans have now lost six running, and nine consecutively at their mountain home — a home skid matched in the franchise's annals only by its inaugural nine of 1993.

FENWAY CONTINUES ITS RESTORATIVE WORK: BOSTONS 5, ORANGE AND BLACK 4, AND THE COUNT AT HOME REACHES THREE RUNNING

A three-run fourth — Wong doubling upon a challenged and overturned call, Gasper and Rafaela cashing in behind him — carried Boston past an early San Francisco lead, and though the visitors crept within one in the seventh on a pair of Boston throwing miscues, Chapman barred the door for his nine-and-twentieth save. Three straight now for the Fenway men, seven of their last ten, and the wild-card cushion holds at a comfortable six and a half games.

NINETEEN RUNS, TWO GRAND SLAMS, AND A LONG EVENING BY THE SOUND: CUBS 19, SEATTLE NINE 2

Arozarena opened Sunday's proceedings precisely as he had opened and closed Saturday's — with a homer, his twentieth, the second consecutive evening he greeted the Chicago starter thus — and thereafter the visitors declined all further courtesy. Conforto answered over the fence, Happ delivered a grand slam in the third, Crow-Armstrong struck his three-and-thirtieth in a nine-run eighth, and the rookie Pedro Ramírez added a second slam of his own before contributing again in a three-run ninth: nineteen runs on seventeen hits, and a seventeen-run verdict that washed away three consecutive defeats at a stroke. Civale collected the win; the Seattle nine will be forgiven for burning the scorecards.

TATIS AND MERRILL SUPPLY THE THUNDER, BUEHLER THE QUIET: FRIARS 8, TWIN CITIES NINE 1

San Diego's evening proceeded from comfort to rout: Tatis hammered his seventeenth homer, Merrill his one-and-twentieth, and a four-run sixth put the matter beyond litigation while Buehler took the decision to eight-and-six. A third consecutive victory keeps the Friars in possession of the National's final wild-card chair, two games clear of Arizona's pursuit with Miami four astern.

TWO HITS ARE NOT ENOUGH TO EAT: ANGELENOS 4, BUCCANEERS 0, AND THE SWEEP IS SEALED

Snell and the Los Angeles relief corps rationed Pittsburgh to two hits the whole afternoon, Ohtani scored the game's first run before some spectators had found their seats, and run-scoring singles by Alek Thomas and Feduccia made the rest academic. A sixth consecutive victory completes the sweep of the Buccaneers and keeps the champions — eighty wins now against one-and-fifty defeats — a single game astern of Milwaukee for the best record in all baseball, with the collision at Atlanta opening tomorrow.

FOUR IN THE SEVENTH REDEEM A SORROWFUL SUNDAY: DESERT NINE 5, QUEEN CITY NINE 3

Cincinnati banked three runs in the third and guarded them into the seventh, whereupon Arizona's patience matured all at once: Ildemaro Vargas tripled two runners home, Carroll lifted the go-ahead sacrifice fly, and four runs crossed in the frame. The victory fell to Loáisiga and the seal to Ginkel, a tonic on the very day the club dispatched Soroka to the infirmary — the ward above has the particulars. The Desert nine remain two games back of San Diego in the wild-card hunt; the Reds' September arithmetic grows grim.

THE TWELVE-YEAR-OLDS DEMANDED A HOMER, AND HARRIS OBLIGED IN THE NINTH: ATLANTAS 4, SUDS MEN 2, AT WILLIAMSPORT

At historic Bowman Field, before an audience whose median age required a bedtime, the ninth Little League Classic went to Atlanta. Michael Harris II, hectored good-naturedly before every at-bat by a delegation of twelve-year-olds demanding a home run ("I let them down," he confessed of the earlier attempts, "so eventually I had to do it"), delivered their commission in the ninth — his one-and-twentieth, off the Milwaukee reliever Ashby — to fatten a lead built on Dubón's ground-rule double and Sean Murphy's single. Mahle took the win and Iglesias the save; Harris had earlier homered in nobody's imagination but the children's, which is rather the point of the fixture. The Suds men, though beaten, retain baseball's best record at one-and-eighty wins, six clear of the Cubs in the Central.

Let the record show a small miracle of stillness: the American's final wild-card chair, whose occupancy this desk has recorded in a different arrangement on seven consecutive mornings, this morning kept its tenants. Texas and Cleveland remain in joint possession, now at five-and-sixty wins apiece, with Toronto a game and a half astern, Minnesota and Baltimore two, and Seattle three — though the reader is cautioned that both incumbents sit below the break-even line, and that Houston shares the West's crown with Texas at the identical figure, a diarchy of the barely solvent unusual even by that division's standards. In the National the seating likewise holds: the Cubs, Philadelphia, and San Diego in the three chairs, Arizona two back of the Friars. The card this evening runs to ten engagements, all verified against the schedule: the Phillies carry their nine-game streak and their westward luggage into Seattle at 9:40 Eastern, Wheeler and his ten victories opposing Gilbert; the Rays visit Detroit; the Cubs, fresh from their nineteen-run sermon, open at Phoenix; and the idle Brewers, Dodgers, and Braves sharpen their knives for tomorrow's grander collisions. Until the morrow's dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.

entry.title: AROZARENA GIVETH, AND AROZARENA TAKETH AWAY: A LEADOFF BLAST, A HOMER STOLEN AT THE WALL, AND THE LAST WORD IN THE NINTH, AS THE MARINERS OF THE SOUND SINK THE BRUINS, 5 TO 4
entry.content:
Is it spring training yet? No — but the championship season is upon us, a finer thing still.

THE MORNING HORSEHIDE HERALD

"Every Score Set Down, No Deed Unsung"

~ Being a Faithful Daily Chronicle of the National Pastime ~

Volume I · No. 46 · Sunday, the Three-and-Twentieth of August, Two Thousand and Twenty-Six

Reporting 15 contests from the day prior.

The Game of the Day

AROZARENA GIVETH, AND AROZARENA TAKETH AWAY: A LEADOFF BLAST, A HOMER STOLEN AT THE WALL, AND THE LAST WORD IN THE NINTH, AS THE MARINERS OF THE SOUND SINK THE BRUINS, 5 TO 4

On the evening appointed for the debutant Anderson, it is the veteran left fielder who writes the game's first sentence, annotates its middle innings with a glove above the fence, and supplies its closing line with a two-run blast — becoming but the seventh man in the recorded annals to open and to end the same game with home runs

Some games are shared among nine men, and some are simply signed. Saturday evening in Seattle bore one signature in three places: at the top, where Randy Arozarena greeted the Cubs' starter Peterson with a leadoff homer to the center-field expanse, a drive of four hundred sixteen feet by the instruments' accounting; in the margin of the third, where the same man went to the wall in left, climbed at the warning track, and drew back over the fence a ball the Cubs' Amaya had every reason to believe was bound for the seats; and at the bottom, where, in the ninth with the tying run aboard, Arozarena struck a second homer to the self-same quarter of center field and ended the affair, five runs to four. The researchers report that only six men before him — Vic Power and Darin Erstad among the ancients, Pete Crow-Armstrong among the moderns — had ever struck a leadoff homer and a walk-off homer in the one game. 'I think it's my biggest game,' the author allowed afterward, 'I didn't expect to come into the game and hit two home runs and rob one.'

The occasion, as this paper has been reporting since Thursday, had been billed for another man entirely: Kade Anderson, the left-hander of two-and-twenty years whom the Pipeline scribes rank the finest pitching pupil in the minors, making his first bow in the majors. The debut was honorable work — five and two-thirds innings on but seventy-two pitches, five hits, two walks, five strikeouts, the first of them Bregman fanned upon a changeup in the opening frame — until the sixth exacted the debutant's tuition: Bregman and Busch struck home runs upon his final two pitches, and Taylor's ground-rule double off the relief made it four runs to two. 'It was just a blast out there,' the young man said, 'and the way the game finished was truly really cool.'

The finish was indeed the thing. In the ninth, against the reliever Webb, Leo Rivas — the same Rivas whose tenth-inning single ended Friday's affair, as this paper related only yesterday — lined a single to right to bring Seattle within one, took his lead from first, and presently crossed with the tying run ahead of Arozarena's thunderbolt: the second consecutive night the Seattle faithful have gone home upon a walk-off verdict. The reliever Rucker was vaulted to the victory, Webb charged with the wreck. The mariners of the Sound now stand two games from the American's final wild-card chair; the Bruins have dropped three running, and their grip on the National's first chair — with Philadelphia's streak at eight, as the card below attests — grows daily less comfortable.

News Around the League

THE MARTE AFFAIR, CONTINUED: A PHOTOGRAPH FROM A CASINO, AND A MANAGER WHO DECLINES TO MAKE A FEDERAL CASE OF IT

The strangest story of the week, chronicled in these columns since Tuesday, produced its latest chapter from an unexpected quarter: the wires report that Ketel Marte, presently on the injured list and taking his treatments at Salt River Fields, was photographed Friday evening at a Scottsdale casino while his clubmates were engaged with the Reds. The manager Torey Lovullo, who but a day earlier spoke of betrayal and of peace in the same breath, chose this time the language of forbearance: 'Ketel's a grown man, and he can make his own decisions,' he offered, noting that men on the injured list take their treatment in the morning and are not required at the yard thereafter, and that no rule of the club was broken. The wires add that Marte kept his Saturday morning rehabilitation appointment, and that he is expected to address his teammates in the coming days. The club, for its part, would doubtless prefer the subject changed: the Snakes dropped Saturday's engagement to the Cincinnatis, as the card below relates, and sit two games from the National's final chair.

THE INFIRMARY WARD: BOTH OF STANTON'S CALVES CONSPIRE AGAINST HIS SEASON, WEATHERS AWAITS THE PHOTOGRAPHS, AND THE CHAMPIONS COUNT TWO RETURNS COMING

The gravest entry issues from the Bronx, where Giancarlo Stanton — six-and-thirty years of age, the active leader in home runs with four hundred six-and-fifty — has strained the left calf in a fall while running the bases, this upon the right calf that has already twice interrupted his year, and the wires allow that the injury may close his 2026 account entire. The manager Boone declines to rule anything out; the ledger records but four-and-twenty games played. His clubmate Ryan Weathers, whose departure from Saturday's defeat after three and a third innings is noted in the card below, will undergo imaging upon a complaining left forearm.

The champions' ward, by contrast, is discharging patients. Tyler Glasnow, his back spasms quieted, is to be activated to take the ball Tuesday in Atlanta — a date this desk has verified against the schedule — and Shohei Ohtani, absent from the mound since early July with the left knee's complaint, threw thirty pitches to live hitters Saturday and could start a game during the home stand that opens the first of September. 'If it were up to Shohei, he'd be in a game in a few days,' the manager Roberts reported, with the air of a man holding the reins on purpose. Elsewhere: Milwaukee's Woodruff begins a throwing program Wednesday with his shoulder spared the knife, and the Mets' Juan Soto, nursing a calf strain of his own, has reported no fresh progress since his wind sprints of a week past.

THE MILESTONE DESK: STEWART RECLAIMS THE RUNS-BATTED-IN LEAD BY A SINGLE TALLY, AND ALVAREZ'S CROWN OF THREE SURVIVES A DEFEAT

The two-horse race this desk has chronicled all week changed noses again Saturday. The Reds' rookie Sal Stewart, granted a full evening's commerce in his club's eleven-run demonstration at Phoenix, drove home the run that lifts him to seven-and-ninety on the season — one clear of the Cardinals' Jordan Walker, whose club could offer him nothing to drive in during the twelve-to-three calamity at Philadelphia. Walker's clubmate Burleson lurks at four-and-ninety, and the question of whether a freshman may lead the major leagues in runs batted in — a thing no rookie has done since 1950 — remains the finest sustained argument of the season's final month.

In the American, Yordan Alvarez's pursuit of the batter's Triple Crown proceeds even where his club stumbles: Houston's Saturday defeat is recorded below, but the big man's figures — .319, six-and-thirty homers, ninety runs driven in — remain first in all three columns, with Simpson of Tampa Bay eleven points astern in average, Caminero one homer back, and Baltimore's Alonso five runs shy on the third table. And in Toronto the strikeout ledger acquires interest: Dylan Cease, whose near-miss is sung in the card below, now owns two hundred nine, within sight of the club record of two hundred eight-and-forty that Robbie Ray set in 2021.

THE ALMANAC DESK: TO WILLIAMSPORT AT LAST — THE NINTH LITTLE LEAGUE CLASSIC, AND A FIRST FOR BOTH NINES ENGAGED

The pilgrimage this paper has been promising all week is come. This evening at ten minutes past seven, Eastern, the Braves and the Brewers repair to Journey Bank Ballpark at historic Bowman Field in Williamsport, Pennsylvania, there to contest the ninth annual Little League Classic before the smallest and sternest jury in baseball — the young players of the Little League World Series, seated a few rows from the field they dream upon. It is the first appearance in the fixture for either franchise, and the occasion will honor the late, great Henry Aaron and his counsel to 'keep swinging' — words the almanac desk is pleased to reprint without amendment. Mahle takes the ball for Atlanta against the left-hander Drohan; the game travels by the ESPN wire. The desk notes besides that this day closes the Players' Weekend program, whose Spider-Man bats and borrowed stirrups enliven the columns below, and that the regular season's final day stands at the twenty-seventh of September — thirty-five days hence, for those keeping the arithmetic.

The Rest of the Card

HITLESS INTO THE SEVENTH, AND THE ROAD STREAK DIES AT TWO-AND-FORTY: TORONTOS 4, PINSTRIPES 3, WITH GUERRERO RESTORED TO THE LINE

Dylan Cease carried a no-hitter into the seventh inning at the Bronx — his second such excursion of the season, the drought of Toronto no-hitters standing at six-and-thirty years since Dave Stieb's — before Wells' run-scoring single spoiled the bid and the shutout in a single blow; the same blow ended Cease's scoreless streak upon the road at two-and-forty innings, second in the expansion age only to Clemens. Eight strikeouts against five walks the ledger shows, two hundred nine on the season, and Lukes' eighth homer in the eighth proved the winning run when García Jr. answered with a two-run shot and Varland barred the door for his nine-and-twentieth save. Vladimir Guerrero Jr., restored from the concussion list precisely as this paper foretold, collected two hits in his return; the losing pitcher Weathers departed after three and a third with the forearm complaint the infirmary ward records. 'What else can I say about him?' Guerrero asked of his ace, and the desk has no improvement to offer.

TWELVE PITCHES, ONE VERDICT: BREW CREW 4, BRAVES 1, AND THE SERIES IS BANKED BEFORE THE TRAIN LEAVES FOR WILLIAMSPORT

Jake Bauers fouled off seven consecutive offerings from the left-hander Pérez in the third, and upon the twelfth pitch of the argument deposited the ball four hundred thirteen feet away for a two-run homer, his three-and-twentieth. 'That might have been the best at-bat of my life,' the batsman confessed, and his manager Murphy pronounced it 'the epitome of draggin' 'em.' Henderson gave six innings of one-run ball for his eighth victory against two defeats, Ashby closed, and Harris' first-inning double — which briefly staked Atlanta — was all the East's leaders would get. At one-and-eighty wins against nine-and-forty defeats, Milwaukee owns the finest ledger in baseball; both nines now entrain for Williamsport, as the almanac desk proclaims.

THE FISH FEED EARLY AND THE SENATORS STARVE LATE: MIAMI 4, WASHINGTON 2

Three runs inside two innings — Lopez's two-run single and Hernández's nineteenth homer — settled the character of the afternoon before Washington had unpacked, and Marsee's eighth homer answered at once when Tena's single had trimmed the margin. Pérez pitched to his seventh victory, Faucher sealed his second save, and the Floridians, winners of two running and nine-and-thirty games at their own yard, sit four from the National's final chair. The Senators have now dropped eight of ten, and the season grows short of mercies.

SEVEN INNINGS, ONE RUN, AND EVERY PERSONAL LEDGER REWRITTEN: PHILS 12, CARDINALS 3, AND THE STREAK IS EIGHT

The young Andrew Painter, sent down to the minors but weeks ago to learn from failure, returned Saturday to administer a lesson: seven innings — the longest outing of his life — a single run, eight strikeouts, twenty swings-and-misses where his previous best was fourteen, and — for the first time in his career — a full hundred pitches, the last of them clocked at 99.6 miles per hour. His employers meanwhile assembled a dozen runs, Harper's three-run homer and Schwarber's eight-and-thirtieth — the National's largest count — the heaviest blows. Eight consecutive victories for the Brotherly Love nine, who sit three behind Atlanta and hold the National's second wild-card chair; the Mound City men, twelve-to-three losers with Wetherholt's homer the lone ornament, must console themselves with the milestone desk's arithmetic.

TROUT STRIKES THE FIRST BLOW AND THE ANAHEIM NINE PAINT ARLINGTON WHITE: ANGELS 3, RANGERS 0

Mike Trout singled home the game's first run in the opening frame, scored its second himself upon Ballesteros' sixth-inning double, and Grissom added a third in the eighth; the pitcher Johnson and the relief corps made the three stand up entire, Watson closing the account. A whitewash is a hard sequel to a walk-off — the Arlington men, delivered so operatically in the tenth on Friday, managed five hits Saturday and no runs at all, and the defeat costs them sole occupancy of the American's final wild-card chair, of which the desk note gives the full accounting.

IT'S GOT TO BE THE STIRRUPS: BALTIMORES 3, SUNSHINE NINE 2, IN TEN, AS BASALLO TIES IT IN BORROWED HOSIERY AND BEAVERS ENDS IT

Before the first pitch at Camden Yards, Tyler O'Neill decreed orange stirrups and white socks for the whole company, and the rookie Samuel Basallo — arriving late — borrowed his pair from the pitcher Bradish. Thus attired, Basallo strode into the eighth as a pinch-hitter with his club two runs down and struck a game-tying homer of four hundred eleven feet, his seventeenth; in the tenth, Dylan Beavers — another man off the bench — doubled home Taveras against the All-Star closer Baker for the walk-off verdict, Baltimore's four-and-thirtieth pinch-hit run driven in of the season, the most in the majors. 'I liked it out there. Guys looked good,' the manager Albernaz ruled. The Baltimores have won two running and stand one game from the American's final chair; the Rays have dropped three running, their lead upon the league trimmed to three games, and McClanahan's five spotless innings go unrewarded.

TWO OUTS BOUGHT DEAR IN THE EIGHTH: ATHLETICS 4, ASTROS 3

Houston led by two entering the eighth on the strength of Varsho's homer and Peña's run-scoring single, whereupon the visitors assembled a three-run recovery from modest materials — Butler's single through a deflection, Heim's run-scoring ground-out — atop Walton's earlier fourth homer. Medina claimed the decision, Alvarado his third save. The Astros, beaten to exactly the break-even line at five-and-sixty apiece, keep the West's first chair by a single game over Texas — whose own whitewash is recorded above — and Alvarez, hitless fortunes notwithstanding, keeps his three crowns, as the milestone desk attests.

FIVE HOMERS ABROAD, TWO OF THEM BY THE MAN THE SOUTH SIDE BOOED: METS 10, WHITE STOCKINGS 5

Luis Robert Jr., nine seasons a White Stocking and a Met since January, returned to the old premises and struck two home runs — four hundred five feet and four hundred seventeen, the boos rising with each — and his mates added three more from Bichette, the rookie Benge, and Torrens in a ten-run demonstration. 'It feels good to hit homers against any team,' Robert allowed, 'but I will say, it did feel good to hit the home runs here.' Warren took the decision in relief; the Central's leaders keep their chair by three and a half games over Cleveland, and the Mets bank a rare road feast.

THE WEB-SLINGER STRIKES AND THE ROYALS MAKE IT SEVEN RUNNING: KANSAS CITY 3, BENGALS 1

Kyle Isbel, having traded Friday's Buzz Lightyear bat for one done up in Spider-Man's livery on Players' Weekend's closing turn, slung his sixth homer into the right-field seats, and the venerable Salvador Perez added his seventeenth of the year; Wacha pitched to his seventh victory, and the ancient Kimbrel recorded his first save of the season. Seven consecutive victories for the Kansas City nine, eight of ten by the ledger, the liveliest late August in the American's lower reaches; the Bengals, with Lee's homer their lone tally, have dropped four running and slip two and a half from the final chair.

THREE RUNS BEFORE HE FOUND HIS FOOTING, THEN EIGHTEEN OF NINETEEN RETIRED: BOYS IN BLUE 4, ALLEGHENYS 3

The Pittsburghs fell upon Tarik Skubal at once — Oneil Cruz's two-run triple the heavy blow of a three-run first — and then the left-hander, acquired from Detroit in the deadline commerce, closed the ledger: eighteen of his final nineteen batters retired, eleven strikeouts across seven innings, the visitors hitless in their last seventeen turns against him. 'That's the guy that we needed,' the manager Roberts pronounced. Tucker's two-run single in the fifth supplied the winning margin, Scott sealed his nineteenth save, and the champions' fifth consecutive victory holds them two games behind Milwaukee on the game's best ledger — with reinforcements coming, as the infirmary ward reports.

NOTHING FOR EIGHT INNINGS, EVERYTHING IN THE NINTH: CRIMSON HOSE 3, BAY NINE 2

Adames and Knizner had homered early, Sandoval — five and two-thirds strong innings in his return from the elbow operation — had kept Boston within reach, and still the Hub men entered the ninth with nothing on their side of the ledger. Then: White's run-scoring single, Sogard's game-tying double off the Monster, and with the sacks full and one out, Abreu — hitless in five, four times a strikeout victim — grounded one down the first-base line and beat the play at the plate for the walk-off, a fielder's choice upheld upon San Francisco's challenge and celebrated by the tearing of the hero's jersey. The one-and-thirtieth comeback victory of Boston's season keeps the second wild-card chair warm; the Bay nine have dropped three running.

HAVE A DAY, BLEDAY: A DOUBLE, A TRIPLE, A SINGLE, A HOMER — THE EIGHTH CYCLE IN THE ANNALS OF CINCINNATI — AND THE REDS ROUT THE SNAKES, 11 TO 5

JJ Bleday assembled his masterpiece one exhibit at a time: a double in the first, a triple in the third, a single in the fifth, and in the sixth the homer that completed the eighth cycle in the long history of the Cincinnati club, the first since Elly De La Cruz's in 2023. ('I'm just like, please, please, God, please go,' the author said of the final exhibit, 'because I top-spun it.') De La Cruz himself went four-for-six with his one-and-twentieth homer and fell only the triple shy of joining him, McLain added a homer, the rookie Stewart drove home the run the milestone desk celebrates, and Lowder took the decision. Eleven runs, the losing streak snapped; for Arizona, Arenado's homer and the Marte business besides, a day best forgotten.

ADELL'S THUNDER TRAVELS WELL AT ALTITUDE: FOREST CITY NINE 4, ROCKIES 3, AND THE CHAIR IS GAINED

Jo Adell's three-run homer in the fourth — his twentieth — did the day's heavy lifting, Bailey singled home insurance in the sixth, and Cleveland then held its breath as Norby's ninth-inning homer drew Colorado within one before Smith closed his three-and-thirtieth save. A third consecutive victory, and with Texas whitewashed at Arlington, the Forest City men wake this morning in shared possession of the American's final wild-card chair — the accounting the desk note completes. The Rockies have dropped five running, and the altitude no longer explains it.

FIVE RUNS SPENT BY THE FOURTH, AND THE MISSION NINE COLLECT SIX UNANSWERED: PADRES 7, MINNESOTANS 5

Minnesota struck three homers inside two innings — Keaschall, Lee, and the rookie Culpepper — and led five runs to one entering the home sixth, whereupon San Diego reclaimed the whole account: Merrill's twentieth homer had kept the hosts breathing, Cronenworth's two-run double crowned a four-run seventh, France singled home the lead, and Tatis added the insurance. Canning profited in relief, Miller sealed his two-and-thirtieth save. The Mission men's second consecutive victory — seven of ten — keeps the National's third wild-card chair; the Minnesotans fall a game from the American's final one.

The arithmetic desk, which has now recorded a different arrangement of the American's final wild-card chair on seven consecutive mornings, reports today's seating as follows: Texas and Cleveland in joint occupancy at four-and-sixty wins apiece — the Rangers whitewashed out of sole possession, the Guardians winners of three running — with Toronto half a game astern, Minnesota and Baltimore one, Seattle two, and Detroit two and a half; not one claimant yet at the break-even line. In the National the chairs hold their tenants — the Cubs first by four games though losers of three running, Philadelphia second with the streak at eight, San Diego third — with Arizona two back, Miami four, and St. Louis four and a half. The card this day runs again to the full fifteen engagements, and the bill of fare is crowned at Williamsport: the Braves and Brewers in the ninth Little League Classic at Bowman Field, ten minutes past seven, Eastern, as the almanac desk relates in full. Before it: at Philadelphia at 1:35, Sánchez and his sixteen victories seek the ninth straight for the Quakers against St. Louis; at Baltimore at the same hour, the Rays send Martinez and his twelve victories against Baz to stanch a three-game wound; in the Bronx, Soriano opposes Rodón; and in Seattle at 4:10, Imanaga is charged with ending both the Bruins' skid and the home nine's walk-off habit. Until the next dispatch, keep your scorecards near and your enthusiasms nearer.
